data.name: Campaign Guide
entries: {@i No Cause for Alarm: Ruins of Bellweather} is a Dungeons & Dragons adventure for four characters, beginning at 3rd level and ending at 16th level. The adventure takes place in Bellweather, a hard-won settlement built against the ruins of a much larger fallen city.

Bellweather grows as the characters reclaim streets, buildings, trade routes, and strongholds. Each success makes the city safer and more prosperous, but recovery also creates new struggles over property, influence, labor, and public trust. Two threats rise with the city: {@b Perrin Cardon}, a human man whose family claims and political ambitions expand with every reclaimed district, and {@b Tyren}, a possessing intelligence that coordinates hostile forces from the shadows.

entries.name: Campaign State — Read Before Preparing the Next Session
entries: Kellan's Well ACTUAL PLAY override: Noren and Veteran are bound and the party rests at scene end. The sluice-repair objective was removed by the DM, and three Bow Gallery Scouts were faced. Council mission payment is not contingent on repairs.

Blackstone is complete; Kellan's Well has been played with the party at level 4. Noren disclosed the royal takeover during the Well mission, and Bellweather's new government is the basis of Chapter 6.

The former Council transferred Bellweather to the Crown. Koven House is Crown HQ; Bishop Brann stayed; Brakkus's Ledger House remains independent. Prepare a roleplay-led return with no compulsory combat.

Pepper is a cleric, not a rogue. She completed one unpaid Council job and owes four paid missions under the former Council's unresolved judgment. Brakkus no longer supervises her house arrest, and the newly arrived Crown is occupied with citywide records; Jord may advise keeping a low profile. Do not force Crown service or an arrest subplot. Jarrock and Pepper's personal conflict continues.

Next return session: Brakkus sits all the PCs down to ask about themselves; Jord and Bishop Brann each have their own perspective on the Crown's changes; Tulcornix Avemvir must arrive late with news that Kaleb's wife is indentured and needs help. No mandatory fight or resistance quest.
Do not use obsolete Council commission and Perrin-as-First-Councilor predictions in the unplayed Chapters 7–17 as facts. See Appendix I for confirmed and unresolved continuity.

This week's start: Noren and his veteran are still captive in Kellan's Well; decide whether to kill, release, or give to city watch before returning to Bellweather. Kill or hand over Noren = out of campaign; release = later underground resistance resource. Cardon Weavehouse street-facing annex holds Elowen under Crown indenture; Tulcornix arrives late with wing injured by work hauling near the annex.

entries.name: Running the Adventure
entries: The campaign follows a repeating rhythm: the characters return to Bellweather, learn what has changed, choose among available problems, venture into the ruins or surrounding lands, and return to a city altered by their decisions.

{@b NPC presentation.} When a named NPC physically enters a scene for the first time, explicitly state species, apparent age, height/build, clothing or gear, at least one memorable physical feature, and a demeanor or voice cue. Keep it to one or two sentences and do not repeat the full description on later appearances unless the NPC's appearance has materially changed.

The Council is an important institution, but it is never the only source of work. Residents, merchants, labor crews, temples, and allied factions can all provide leads. When the characters reject one route, present another rather than forcing them back toward a single patron.

entries.name: The Title: No Cause for Alarm
entries: The phrase {@b no cause for alarm} appears occasionally in Bellweather's public notices and official reassurances. Early in the adventure it is mundane civic language. As danger grows, the same words become increasingly charged by who uses them, what they minimize, and who bears the consequences.
Use the phrase sparingly. It should recur at important turning points rather than become a catchphrase.

entries.name: Milestones
entries: Characters gain levels when their actions materially change Bellweather's position, secure a major district, break an enemy advantage, or complete a decisive political or military objective. Recommended levels appear at the start of each chapter.

entries.name: Reclamation Frontier
entries: Bellweather is not an open city surrounded by uncontrolled ruins. Its inhabited core is protected by a shifting reclamation frontier made from repaired remnants of the old city walls, masonry barricades, deliberately collapsed streets, timber works, watch posts, and guarded gates. Beyond that line, the ruins are not assumed safe.

Any district, stronghold, route, or site that the campaign describes as needing to be cleared, secured, reclaimed, reopened, or reconquered begins outside Bellweather's dependable security unless a chapter explicitly says otherwise. Residents may know of it, salvage from its edges, or travel near it, but routine civilian movement and patrols do not extend through it.

items: {@b Secured.} Inside Bellweather's dependable protection. Streets are patrolled, ordinary residents can travel with reasonable confidence, and repaired defenses or controlled approaches separate the area from unreclaimed ruins.
{@b Contested.} On the active frontier. Scouts, workers, salvagers, monsters, criminals, or hostile forces may all be present. Bellweather can reach the area, but does not control it reliably.

{@b Unreclaimed.} Beyond the city's dependable reach. No routine patrol or civilian safety is assumed, and hostile creatures or factions can occupy the area without immediately threatening the inhabited core because controlled approaches, barriers, distance, or terrain keep them outside the secured line.

entries: When the characters complete the objective that secures a district, the city's visible frontier changes. Barricades move, gates reopen, walls are patched, patrols advance, workers enter, traffic resumes, and the reclaimed area becomes part of everyday Bellweather. A geographically isolated objective instead becomes a fortified reclaimed outpost connected to Bellweather by a secured route; the map should not force the defensive perimeter into an implausible shape merely to include it.

Cleared does not mean sterile. Individual hazards, crimes, hidden creatures, political disputes, or damaged buildings can remain in a secured district. The distinction is whether Bellweather can maintain ordinary control there without treating every trip as an expedition.

Player-facing city maps should be updated after meaningful reclamation milestones. Show the current secured boundary, controlled gates or checkpoints, newly opened routes, reclaimed districts, and the broad status of known frontier areas. Do not reveal undiscovered threats, secret occupants, or DM-only information merely because the map changes.

entries.name: Treasure
entries: Treasure favors memorable rewards over large piles of interchangeable magic items. Permanent magic should usually be tied to a recovered heirloom, named location, faction reward, or story consequence. Coin, art objects, consumables, salvage, and story rewards remain useful throughout the adventure.

The campaign is balanced for four characters. By about 5th level, the party should have roughly four meaningful uncommon permanent items across the group; rare items begin appearing in the middle tiers, very rare items become major rewards in the high tiers, and legendary items remain story-specific.

Use each chapter's Rewards section for its intended reward budget and Appendix B: Rewards and Loot for cache tables, catch-up guidance, attunement guardrails, and salvage ownership. Named story relics remain in place even when generic treasure quantities are superseded.

entries.name: Campaign Economy
entries: Bellweather uses an adventurer-scale economy. Do not track routine rations, ordinary ammunition, or incidental daily meals. Charge normally for lodging, transportation, spellcasting, hirelings, guides, major services, equipment, potions purchased in town, and other meaningful discretionary expenses.

{@b Price anchors.} Use the campaign shop prices as the baseline: studded leather 45 gp, splint 200 gp, breastplate 400 gp, half plate 750 gp, plate 1,500 gp, a Potion of Healing 50 gp, and magic-item value anchors of roughly 100 gp common, 400 gp uncommon, 4,000 gp rare, 40,000 gp very rare, and 200,000 gp legendary. Availability remains separate from affordability; Bellweather does not automatically stock every magic item.

{@b Wealth pacing.} A character who saves a substantial share of earnings should be able to afford splint by about level 4, breastplate by levels 4–5, half plate by levels 5–6, and plate by levels 7–8. By level 10, a character who has saved aggressively can plausibly purchase a rare item if one is actually available. Later rewards rise sharply because mundane equipment should no longer be the principal constraint.

entries.caption: Suggested Cumulative Spendable Wealth per Character

entries: {@b Ownership and salvage.} Identifiable private property, civic records, religious relics, and Council equipment are not ordinary loot. Returning them earns payment, favors, reputation, access, or restitution. Unclaimed coin, hostile-faction funds, trade bars, gems, jewelry, explicitly abandoned salvage, and awarded valuables are normal treasure. This distinction reinforces Bellweather’s disputes over ownership without turning every ruin into unrestricted salvage.

{@b Permanent magic.} Permanent items remain curated. Do not convert every monetary reward into unrestricted magic-item shopping. Shops may carry common and uncommon items when appropriate; rare and better items usually require reputation, a specialist seller, commission, auction, faction access, or a specific opportunity.

entries.name: Character Threads
entries: These are {@b optional pressure points}, not hidden explanations for the main plot.
Jarrock

Bellweather's reclamation should repeatedly show Jarrock different ways class power operates: workers risking their lives for property they cannot own, old families reclaiming inherited wealth, merchants buying influence, Council policies that are legal but unequal, and Brakkus demonstrating that wealth or status does not automatically make a person abusive. The campaign should give Jarrock reasons to form his own beliefs about unjust rulers; it should never tell him that he is destined to kill a king and queen.
Aaron Dunamus

Aaron's history with domination remains separate from Tyren and Bellweather's political story. Situations involving coercion, debt, forced service, magical control, or people being treated as property can resonate with him because of his experience under Dimidicus. His personal threads—Dimidicus, the spawn he left behind, and the mysterious figure who freed him—should appear intermittently and never be revealed as secret pieces of Bellweather's main conspiracy.

entries.name: Jarrock — Rena Dask Labor Thread
entries: Keep Jarrock's class-and-power theme as a small recurring subplot rather than a second main plot. {@b Rena Dask}, a dwarf stonemason and informal crew representative, appears in two or three scenes as Bellweather expands.
First beat: Rena is one of the workers risking injury to survey and reopen property in the Slums. She asks who benefits when workers make a district valuable enough for someone else to claim.

Second beat: around the Cardon Weavehouse, Rena pushes for compensation, safety guarantees, or a public share of recovered value for the crews doing the reclamation. She is practical, not doctrinaire, and accepts compromise when it materially helps workers.

Third beat: during the Mansion property precedents, Rena challenges Jarrock to distinguish between opposing abusive power and simply distrusting whoever currently holds power. She can also be wrong: she may defend a worker shortcut, overestimate what Bellweather can afford, or underestimate a legitimate ownership claim. The point is to make Jarrock decide what he believes, not to hand him the correct answer.

entries.name: Story Overview
entries: Fifty years ago, Bellweather fell to an alliance of monstrous armies whose cooperation seemed impossible. A new settlement has since established a protected foothold and begun reclaiming the old city. The Council hires adventurers because it lacks the manpower to clear every block itself.

As the characters reclaim Bellweather, they hear of a feared {@b Boss} holding otherwise fractious forces together. At the same time, Perrin Cardon—a human minor Council member descended from one of Old Bellweather's wealthy merchant houses—quietly uses the recovery to restore his family fortune and increase his political influence.

The two stories tighten around the {@b Radiant Well}, a source of power sought by Cardon and already exploited by Tyren, the possessing intelligence who turns a controlled host into the apparent “Boss.” The characters eventually face both a political betrayal inside Bellweather and the supernatural power controlling its enemies.

entries.name: The Boss, Tyren, and Soren
entries: {@b The Boss} is the title soldiers, traders, and frightened residents use for the apparently singular ruler coordinating Old Bellweather's hostile factions. Early in the campaign, almost nobody understands that the title hides two beings: {@b Tyren}, a possessing intelligence, and {@b Soren}, the bronze-dragon host he eventually controls.

Before the possession reveal, rumors and uninformed NPCs may simply say {@b the Boss}. After Marren Library establishes possession, DM-facing text should treat Tyren as the true intelligence behind that title. Uninformed NPCs can continue using the old name. Soren's identity as the current host is not confirmed until the late campaign.

data.name: Chapter 1: The Storm
entries: {@b Recommended level:} 3

entries.name: Chapter Overview
entries: {@b Chapter purpose.} Bring four strangers together through a rescue, establish Ledger House, and let the players choose their first route into the Slums.

entries.name: Running the Chapter
entries: {@b Primary objectives.} Rescue trapped residents; stabilize a collapsing route; recover supplies only if lives are secure.
{@b Player agency.} Ledger House becomes the shared refuge. Brakkus notices the group and points out that the Council pays capable people to reclaim the ruins.
{@b Fail forward.} Failed checks cost time, gear, or create injuries; they do not make the rescue impossible.

{@b Rest and pressure.} Safe long rests are available back at Ledger House. Inside the active adventure site, resting gives opposing factions time to reposition unless the characters secure a defensible refuge.

entries.name: Scene 1: The Storm Rescue
The Storm Breaks
entries: The road into Bellweather has become a ribbon of mud beneath a black, churning sky. Rain lashes sideways hard enough to sting. Ahead, the half-rebuilt walls of the city appear and vanish behind sheets of water, their lanterns little more than blurred yellow smears in the storm.

A crack of thunder rolls over the road. A draft horse screams. Fifty feet ahead, a wagon slews sideways as one wheel drops into a washout, throwing the driver into the mud and pinning another traveler beneath the tilted bed. At the same moment, brown runoff bursts across the roadside ditch, cutting off two laborers trying to reach higher ground. From the ruined shell of a nearby stone building comes the sharp report of timber splitting. A family sheltering beneath its remaining awning looks up as the roof begins to sag.
For a few seconds, everyone on the road freezes. Then all three disasters begin to get worse at once.

The characters are close enough to reach any of the three emergencies. They need not know one another before the storm; the situation gives them an immediate reason to act together. Do not roll initiative. Ask each player what their character does, resolve the most urgent actions, then move quickly around the table as conditions change.

entries.name: The Three Emergencies
entries: The storm creates three simultaneous problems within roughly 100 feet of one another. Characters can split up or concentrate on one problem at a time. Clever use of spells, equipment, class features, or the environment can solve an obstacle without a check when appropriate.

entries.name: 1. The Overturned Wagon
entries: A two-horse freight wagon has tipped into a washout. The driver is conscious but dazed in the mud. A second traveler is trapped beneath the wagon bed while one terrified horse kicks against tangled traces.

A character can calm or cut free the horse, brace the wagon, lever the bed upward, dig mud away from the trapped traveler, or attempt another reasonable solution. Typical checks include DC 12 Strength (Athletics), DC 12 Wisdom (Animal Handling), or DC 13 Dexterity using appropriate tools or rope.

If no one addresses the horse before the scene advances, it lashes out in panic. One nearby creature must succeed on a DC 12 Dexterity saving throw or take 1d6 bludgeoning damage and be knocked prone.

entries.name: 2. The Flooded Ditch
entries: Two reclamation laborers are stranded on the far side of a drainage ditch that has become a fast, waist-deep torrent. The old plank crossing tears loose moments after the characters arrive.

Characters might throw a rope, anchor a line, wade across, improvise a bridge, use magic, or reach the laborers from higher ground. Typical checks include DC 12 Strength (Athletics) to cross with a secured line, DC 12 Dexterity to throw or secure a rope under pressure, or DC 13 Wisdom (Survival) to identify a safer crossing point.

A character swept into the runoff is carried 20 feet and takes 1d6 bludgeoning damage from debris before catching on rubble or being pulled free. No civilian is simply washed away because of a single failed roll.

entries.name: 3. The Failing Shelter
entries: A family of three has taken cover beneath the surviving awning of an old roadside structure. Water is pouring through the upper masonry, and each gust shifts the cracked support posts. The structure will partially collapse unless the family is moved or the roof is stabilized.

Characters can evacuate the family, shore up the supports, redirect runoff, clear a safer route through the rubble, or use magic to protect them. Typical checks include DC 12 Strength (Athletics), DC 12 Intelligence using mason's or carpenter's tools, or DC 13 Wisdom (Perception) to identify which section will fall first.
On a complication, falling debris deals 1d6 bludgeoning damage to a character who remains under the awning, or destroys a piece of unattended mundane gear.

entries.name: Resolving the Rescue
entries: Track the rescue as a group challenge. The party needs 6 successes before suffering 3 complications. A single action can earn a success if it materially improves the situation; a particularly effective spell or plan can earn a success automatically.

A failed check does not erase progress. Instead, introduce a complication: a character takes 1d6 damage, a rope or tool is lost, the flood shifts position, the wagon settles deeper, falling debris creates a new obstacle, or precious time is lost. After the third complication, the rescue still succeeds, but the group reaches Bellweather battered and with an additional cost chosen from the complication list.

The purpose of the scene is not to test whether innocent people live or die on a handful of opening rolls. It is to show the characters solving a fast-moving emergency together while establishing the storm as a real threat.

entries.name: Scene 2: Entering Bellweather
entries: Once the immediate dangers are under control, Bellweather guards and local workers arrive from the gate with lanterns, ropes, and handcarts. They take charge of the injured and direct everyone displaced by the storm toward Ledger House, one of the few buildings in the district large enough to shelter a crowd.

The rescued travelers and laborers remember the characters' help. Unless the party behaved recklessly or cruelly, word reaches Ledger House before they do that four strangers worked together to keep people alive on the road.

entries.name: Approaching Bellweather
entries: Beyond the gate, Bellweather is all wet stone, canvas tarps, shouted instructions, and lantern light reflected in standing water. Reclamation crews are already clearing drains and bracing damaged walls. Someone points down a crowded street toward a broad, warmly lit building with people packed beneath its eaves.
‘Ledger House,’ the worker says. ‘If you've got nowhere dry to be, that's where you go.’

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Sera Venn, a rescued laborer, mentions a survey crew missing in the Slums.
Jorn Milar, a merchant whose wagon was saved, offers 75 gp to recover a strongbox lost near the eastern ruins.

A city worker says the Council has posted an immediate reclamation contract: {@b 75 gp per person} for capable escorts who can accompany the survey crew, mark hazards, and help reopen a route through the Slums.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: These are parallel hooks. The party needs only one; a Council visit is never mandatory.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: If the characters ignore all three, storm damage later exposes a breach toward the Slums and trapped workers call for help.

entries.name: Scene 3: Ledger House
entries: After the rescue, locals funnel displaced people toward {@b Ledger House}, an established inn and boarding house in Reclaimed Bellweather. Its proprietor, {@creature Brakkus Ledgerhelm|NCFA}, is an older half-orc and retired {@b level 16 Oath of Devotion paladin of Torm}. He is broad-shouldered, scarred, practical, dry, observant, and generous without being sentimental. The calm way he moves through a crowded emergency suggests long experience with danger, but he does not advertise what he once did for a living.
For Brakkus's combat statistics, see {@creature Brakkus Ledgerhelm|NCFA}. He intervenes only when Ledger House, its staff, or its guests face serious danger.

{@creature Brakkus Ledgerhelm|NCFA|Brakkus} feeds people, finds dry blankets, and quietly watches the adventurers work together. Ledger House is deliberately a safe place for travelers, workers, refugees, and anyone else who needs shelter. Brakkus holds no civic office and assigns no official work. He is a steady local contact and the keeper of a reliable refuge.

entries.name: What the Characters See
entries: Wet workers crowd the fire with boots and coats spread wherever they can dry. A displaced resident sleeps upright in a chair while someone quietly opens another room for temporary bedding. Staff carry bowls of stew and dry blankets through the common room without asking who can pay.
Brakkus moves through the room like someone used to emergencies: directing traffic, checking on the injured, remembering who needs food, and making certain nobody is left outside in the storm.
When the immediate crisis settles, Brakkus mentions several ways capable people can find work in Bellweather, including the Council's reclamation contracts:

entries.name: Brakkus Line Prompts
entries: “Travelers. Welcome to Ledger House. It’s been a long night. You’ve done some good work. Please stay here. Have a nice, warm night, and we’ll talk in the morning.”
“You worked together pretty well out there. Better than most people who’ve known each other ten years.”
“Four strangers don’t usually start pulling people out of trouble together unless they’re either very good people or very bad planners.”
“Council’s paying crews to work the old districts. Private crews are hiring too. And half the people in this room probably have something they need done.”
“If you’re looking for work while the roads dry, pick whichever problem bothers you most.”
If asked about Bellweather’s rebuilding: “Everybody likes rebuilding. Arguments start when something worth owning gets rebuilt.”

The characters can rest at Ledger House before choosing what to do next. The Council's first suitable assignment is reclamation work in the {@b Slums}, but the Slums can also be reached through a private survey crew, a missing-worker request, a merchant escort job, or simple exploration. The Council is the official route, not a mandatory one.

entries.name: No Cause for Alarm Beat
entries: The morning after the storm, a Council notice is posted near the gate and market:
{@b PUBLIC NOTICE:} Storm damage remains localized. Reclamation crews are assessing affected structures. Trade and Council business will continue as scheduled. {@b There is no cause for alarm.}

The notice is not sinister. It is exactly the sort of reassurance a fragile frontier settlement would issue to prevent panic and protect trade. That is why the phrase works. Brakkus reads it, glances at whatever part of Ledger House is still dripping, and says only, {@b "Good to know."}
Allow the phrase to pass without emphasis; its significance should emerge through repetition and circumstance.

entries.name: Running Time
entries: Keep the storm, introductions, and Ledger House to roughly 30–45 minutes. The rest of the session should carry the characters into their first Slums objective.

entries.name: Scene 4: Choosing a Lead
entries: The party can follow whichever problem interests them most. Sera Venn points them toward the missing survey crew, Jorn Milar pays for recovery of his strongbox, and the Council posts an immediate {@b 75 gp-per-person} reclamation contract. None of these routes is mandatory.
Once the characters choose a reason to enter the Slums, let them rest if they want and begin Chapter 3 when the roads are passable.

entries.name: Transition to Chapter 3
entries: After the storm eases enough for travel, the chosen hook leads the party into the Slums. Chapter 2 can be used before or after the expedition to introduce Bellweather in greater detail.

entries.name: Rewards
entries: These rewards are party totals for the campaign's four-character party.

items: {@b Spendable wealth.} 25–50 gp in gratitude, supplies, or waived lodging.
{@b Consumables.} 1 minor healing consumable.
{@b Permanent magic.} None automatically.
{@b Story reward.} Free lodging at Ledger House during the immediate aftermath and a stronger connection to Brakkus Ledgerhelm.

data.name: Chapter 2: Reclaimed Bellweather

entries.name: Maps
entries: The approved Crown-era overview is the authoritative current geography of Bellweather after reclamation of the South Ward and establishment of Crown control. Use the original map as historical reference only; do not substitute regenerated layouts.
{@b Recommended level:} 3–16 (recurring hub)

entries.name: Chapter Overview
entries: {@b Chapter purpose.} Make Reclaimed Bellweather a usable hub with recurring services, politics, downtime, and visible consequences.
This chapter is the campaign hub rather than a single expedition. Run it between adventures whenever the characters return to Bellweather.
Brakkus remains a recurring ally and observer of the city’s changes, but the characters—not Brakkus—drive the campaign.

entries.name: Running the Chapter
entries: {@b Primary objectives.} Social exploration, shopping, rumors, Council negotiation, downtime.
{@b Player agency.} Safe long rests at Ledger House. Use one downtime beat between expeditions.
{@b Fail forward.} A poor social check changes price, access, or attitude; it does not erase necessary campaign information.

{@b Rest and pressure.} Safe long rests are available back at Ledger House. Inside the active adventure site, resting gives opposing factions time to reposition unless the characters secure a defensible refuge.

entries.name: Table-Ready Use
entries: Reclaimed Bellweather is a safe base, not an adventure site. Use it for downtime, rumors, shopping, Council negotiations, and consequences from reclamation. {@b Ledger House is the default party home.} Violence here should bring a fast, overwhelming guard response rather than become a combat encounter.

entries.name: Ledger House
entries: Ledger House replaces the need for a generic anonymous inn as the characters' emotional home base. It exists alongside the Council, market, temples, docks, and other civic institutions.

{@creature Brakkus Ledgerhelm|NCFA} owns the house. Brakkus is a roughly forty-eight-year-old half-orc, a retired adventurer and mercenary, and a {@b level 16 Oath of Devotion paladin of Torm}. His adventuring career is behind him by choice, not because he has become frail. He knows laborers, merchants, guards, boat crews, refugees, and old families, and he often understands the human consequences of Council decisions before the Council does. He is not a political mouthpiece, regular quest-giver, or DMPC. He is simply difficult to impress, difficult to fool, and extremely capable of protecting the people under his roof.

Brakkus was raised in the Ironfang Clan by the warlord Korgak and his captive human mother, Elena, a librarian who secretly taught him to read and filled his childhood with stories of duty and Torm the True. After Elena died when Korgak refused her proper care, Brakkus abandoned his father's bloodline and took the name Ledgerhelm in her memory. Years later, High Justiciar Vance Halford trained him as a paladin and witnessed his Oath of Devotion. His signature longsword, {@item The Appendix|NCFA}, was given to him by Vance and named in honor of Elena's love of books.

Ledger House is the culmination of that history: a business, but also a deliberately maintained refuge. Brakkus tolerates ordinary adventurer foolishness. He does not tolerate serious violence against his staff, patrons, or guests. If a scene genuinely requires combat, use his stat block below; otherwise keep his power in the background.

As Bellweather is reclaimed, Ledger House should visibly change: busier common rooms, new workers, displaced families, visiting officials, rival adventurers, merchants, petitioners, and people celebrating or resenting the city's growth.

entries.name: Brakkus Ledgerhelm
entries: Use {@creature Brakkus Ledgerhelm|NCFA} whenever Brakkus enters combat. The entry below summarizes his role in Ledger House and the circumstances under which he fights.

entries.name: DM Use
entries: Brakkus is a home-base NPC, not a companion character. Use this stat block when trouble reaches Ledger House, when Brakkus must protect civilians, or in another exceptional scene where his combat ability matters. His default priorities are {@b protect civilians, stabilize downed allies, contain the threat, then defeat the aggressor}. He uses restraint against ordinary troublemakers and lethal force only when the danger warrants it.
{@creature Brakkus Ledgerhelm|NCFA} {@i Medium Humanoid (Half-Orc), Lawful Good}
{@b Armor Class} 24 (Efreeti Chain Mail, +2 Shield, Defense) {@b Hit Points} 200 {@b Speed} 30 ft.

{@b Saving Throws} Wis +9, Cha +13 {@b Skills} Insight +5, Intimidation +9, Persuasion +9, Religion +4 {@b Damage Immunities} fire {@b Senses} darkvision 60 ft., passive Perception 10 {@b Languages} Common, Orc, Primordial {@b Proficiency Bonus} +5

entries.name: Traits
entries: {@b Aura of Protection.} While Brakkus is conscious, he and friendly creatures within 10 feet of him gain a +4 bonus to saving throws.
{@b Aura of Courage.} While Brakkus is conscious, he and friendly creatures within 10 feet of him can't be Frightened.
{@b Aura of Devotion.} While Brakkus is conscious, he and friendly creatures within 10 feet of him can't be Charmed.
{@b Purity of Spirit.} Brakkus is continuously under the effects of {@spell Protection from Evil and Good|XPHB}.
{@b Relentless Endurance (1/Long Rest).} When Brakkus is reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, he drops to 1 hit point instead.

{@b Lay on Hands (80 HP/Long Rest).} Brakkus has a pool of 80 hit points of healing. As an action, he can touch a creature and restore any number of hit points remaining in the pool. He can instead spend 5 points to cure one disease or neutralize one poison affecting the target.
{@b Fire Walker.} Brakkus can stand on and move across molten rock as if it were solid ground.

entries.name: Actions
entries: {@b Multiattack.} Brakkus makes two attacks with {@item The Appendix|NCFA}.
{@b The Appendix.} {@i Melee Weapon Attack:} +12 to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@i Hit:} 11 (1d8 + 7) slashing damage plus 2 (1d4) radiant damage. The Appendix is a +3 magic longsword.

{@b Divine Smite.} When Brakkus hits a creature with The Appendix, he can expend a spell slot to deal additional radiant damage: 2d8 with a 1st-level slot, 3d8 with a 2nd-level slot, 4d8 with a 3rd-level slot, or 5d8 with a 4th-level slot. The damage increases by 1d8 against a Fiend or Undead, subject to the normal Divine Smite maximum.

{@b Sacred Flame.} One creature Brakkus can see within 60 feet must succeed on a DC 17 Dexterity saving throw or take 13 (3d8) radiant damage. The target gains no benefit from Half Cover or Three-Quarters Cover for this save.
{@b Word of Radiance.} Each creature of Brakkus's choice within 5 feet of him must succeed on a DC 17 Constitution saving throw or take 10 (3d6) radiant damage.

entries.name: Channel Divinity (1/Short or Long Rest)
entries: {@b Sacred Weapon.} As an action, Brakkus imbues The Appendix with positive energy for 1 minute. He adds his Charisma modifier (+4) to attack rolls made with the weapon, raising its attack bonus to +16, and the weapon emits bright light in a 20-foot radius and dim light for another 20 feet.

{@b Turn the Unholy.} As an action, Brakkus presents his holy symbol. Each Fiend or Undead within 30 feet that can see or hear him must succeed on a DC 17 Wisdom saving throw or be Turned for 1 minute or until it takes damage.

entries.name: Reaction
entries: {@b Shield (1/Long Rest).} When Brakkus is hit by an attack roll or targeted by {@spell Magic Missile|XPHB}, he casts {@spell Shield|XPHB}. Until the start of his next turn, his AC becomes 29, including against the triggering attack, and he takes no damage from {@spell Magic Missile|XPHB}.

entries.name: Spellcasting
entries: Brakkus's spellcasting ability is Charisma (spell save {@b DC 17}, {@b +9} to hit with spell attacks). For DM use, keep his combat spell list compact rather than preparing a full PC spell sheet.

{@b At will:} {@i Sacred Flame, Word of Radiance} {@b 1/Long Rest:} {@spell Shield|XPHB} (from Magic Initiate) {@b Prepared Paladin Spells (use spell slots):} {@i Lesser Restoration, Zone of Truth, Beacon of Hope, Dispel Magic, Freedom of Movement, Guardian of Faith} {@b Spell Slots:} 1st level (4), 2nd level (3), 3rd level (3), 4th level (2)

entries.name: Ledger House Trouble
entries: Brakkus tolerates arguments, drunkenness, broken furniture, card cheating, and other ordinary adventurer nonsense as an innkeeper problem. Threatening staff or patrons, attacking civilians, or using dangerous magic in the common room becomes a paladin problem. He normally attempts to end such a fight without killing anyone.

entries.name: The Appendix — Custom Item
entries: {@item The Appendix|NCFA} is Brakkus Ledgerhelm's signature weapon, given to him by High Justiciar Vance Halford and named in honor of Elena's love of books. The Appendix is a named magic weapon with the properties listed below.

items: {@b Weapon (longsword), very rare}
{@b Magic Bonus:} +3 to attack and damage rolls
{@b Radiant Edge:} On a hit, the weapon deals an extra {@b 1d4 radiant damage}.
{@b Campaign Source Tag:} {@item The Appendix|NCFA}

entries: The item does not require attunement unless the adventure later deliberately changes that property.

Reclaimed Bellweather is the party's recurring civic hub: a place to rest, shop, gather rumors, negotiate with the Council, pursue downtime, and see the consequences of earlier choices. Violence is possible, but the district is heavily policed and most conflicts here are social, legal, or political rather than dungeon encounters. Use the locations below to make the city feel inhabited between expeditions.

entries.name: Filling In the Reclaimed Quarter
entries: Use any compact city layout you prefer for the safe quarter. Most unnamed buildings fall into three categories: vacant structures, residences, and warehouses.

{@b Vacant structures.} These may shelter squatters, displaced families, thieves, rival adventurers, or enemy agents. Species never determines whether someone is suspicious. If an actual agent of a hostile faction is discovered, the Council pays for actionable intelligence or a lawful capture; it does not post ancestry-based corpse bounties.
{@b Residences.} Entering a private home without permission brings an understandably hostile response and a quick visit from the Watch.

{@b Warehouses.} These contain ordinary trade goods—dried fish, cloth, potatoes, lumber, wine, salt, copper, iron, baskets of lime, etc. Most warehouses hold ordinary trade goods. If a warehouse matters to the story, place one identifiable valuable or piece of evidence there deliberately rather than rolling for it. Stolen civic or private property can create legal and reputation consequences.

entries.name: The Stockade Wall
entries: The stockade is practical rather than grand: patched timber, fresh braces, signal lanterns, and constant foot traffic. Two patrol teams are normally visible from any gate. During daylight the gates are open to residents, registered workers, merchants, and Council-approved reclamation crews. At night they close except for emergencies. If violence breaks out, nearby {@creature Guard|XMM|Guards} contain the scene while runners summon a {@creature Veteran|XMM} officer and additional support. The purpose of the wall is to protect people, not to create an infinite reinforcement encounter.

entries.name: The Docks
entries: There are always 0-2 ships present and 3 small boats that can provide ferry service to Toren Isle. The boatmen are always good for a general rumor about Bellweather. They also have one piece of specific information: “There ain’t no point in tryin’ to row up the river, lubber. ‘Tis poison sure, through and through. Why’d eat yer planking right out for sure it would! It’s a most unnatural fouling, I’ll warrant ye.” The shops near the docks actually form a small market. Just who or what is there varies greatly. There will usually be {@b 2–8 temporary stalls or shops}. The table below lists what might appear. 2-15: Fishmonger 16: Spice merchant 17: Tinker 18: Alchemist—can sell poisons and healing potions. 19: General merchant—can sell most adventuring supplies at costs below those of merchants in town. 20: Itinerant priest—use the {@creature Priest|XMM} stat block. For those willing to listen to the sermon, the priest can provide modest healing for a donation.

entries.name: Rooms and Inns
entries: {@b The Cracked Crown.} Bellweather's quietest and most expensive inn attracts Council staff, prosperous merchants, visiting advocates, and people who value privacy. Rooms cost {@b 5 gp per night}. Security is good, but wealthy guests also attract professional thieves. Use the Crown when the party needs access to officials away from the Council chamber.

{@b Nat Wyler's Bell.} A crowded, inexpensive inn near the edge of the reclaimed district. Private rooms cost {@b 1 gp per night} and common-room sleeping costs {@b 1 sp}. The Bell is neutral ground for guides, laborers, caravan guards, scouts, and people looking for dangerous work. Patrons strongly discourage theft inside because everyone depends on the place as a safe meeting point.

{@b The Bitter Blade.} A waterfront inn favored by political malcontents, opportunists, sailors, and travelers who want quick access to the docks. Rooms cost {@b 2 gp per night}. The innkeeper is unreliable but well informed; rumors here often concern regional roads, shipping, and dissatisfaction with the Council.

entries.name: Outfitters
entries: {@b Ian Corben, Grocer.} Sells ordinary provisions, lamp oil, household goods, rope, sacks, preserved food, and similar supplies at normal prices.

{@b Maten the Smith.} Bellweather's best armorer and weaponsmith. He keeps limited finished stock but accepts commissions. Custom work costs about 50 percent more than standard gear and normally takes 1–3 weeks. He can refit equipment for different body plans.

{@b Joren Viton, Smith.} Keeps a much larger inventory than Maten but focuses on practical, mass-produced equipment. His gear is mechanically normal; the distinction is reputation and finish, not hidden breakage rules.
{@b Ersten the Farrier.} Sells mounts, tack, feed, and stable services. Mounts cost more than in established cities because nearly everything must be imported.

{@b Jeron Melven, Pawnbroker.} Buys used equipment, jewelry, salvage, and goods of uncertain provenance. He asks few questions, which means characters who knowingly traffic stolen property may later attract a watch investigation.

entries.name: The Slum Market
entries: The open market changes daily. It is a useful place to introduce rumors, temporary merchants, unusual supplies, and minor complications without creating a shopping minigame.

items: {@b Weller the Chandler} sells oddments and one or two unidentified consumables. He is not knowingly fraudulent; his problem is poor records. An Arcana check, {@spell Identify|XPHB}, or a reputable alchemist can verify an item before purchase.
{@b Alden the Wine-Seller} knows local gossip. A drink and {@b 5 gp} buys ordinary rumors; {@b 25 gp} buys a useful lead about a specific district when such information plausibly exists.
{@b Toren the Proselytizer} is a wandering {@creature Priest|XMM} who provides modest healing or restorative magic in exchange for a donation.
{@b Uton the Map Maker} sells maps of varying age and accuracy. Expensive maps are not automatically perfect, but they contain more current annotations and safer routes.

entries.name: The Jail
entries: Bellweather's jail is secure but ordinary. Arrested characters receive charges, an opportunity to speak with an advocate or Council representative, and consequences proportionate to the offense. The Council may offer community service or a dangerous civic assignment as part of a sentence, but accepting a quest is never the only route out of jail and guards do not require implausible bribes.

entries.name: The Council Chamber
entries: The Council posts reclamation contracts publicly. Taking a notice reserves the job for a short period, but characters can also attend a session, ask questions, negotiate terms, or propose alternatives.
The core Council is intentionally multi-species and politically mixed:

items: {@b Ulric Evern}, a well-dressed human in his late fifties or early sixties with silvering dark hair, a neatly trimmed beard, a tailored dark coat, a signet ring, and immaculate boots. He is the senior councilor and budget hawk: a hard bargainer suspicious of open-ended expenses.

{@b Wern Ursen}, a tall, lean elf with practical dark hair, a weathered face, and old scars around the jaw and temple. He wears functional, well-maintained plate armor bearing the Bellweather city crest. A former mercenary captain, he oversees defense and infrastructure.

{@b Bishop Brann}, an older dwarf cleric, broad and heavyset, with a thick gray-white beard kept neatly braided, layered clerical robes over practical mail, a holy symbol worn openly, warm eyes, and large scarred hands. He focuses on public welfare, burial rights, healing, and humane treatment of prisoners.

{@b Perrin Cardon}, a human in his thirties or early forties who is always very well dressed: perfectly fitted clothing, expensive fabrics, polished boots, carefully styled hair, and a subtle family pin or gold chain. Charming rather than foppish, he is an ambitious heir to an old merchant family.

entries: Councilors disagree. Evidence, reputation, public support, and economic consequences can change votes. The Council is not a single NPC with one predetermined answer.

entries.name: The Temple
entries: Bellweather's temporary civic temple serves multiple faiths until larger sanctuaries are reclaimed. {@b Bishop Brann} and several {@b Acolytes} provide ordinary healing, funeral rites, and spiritual support. Significant magic requires a donation, a favor, or access to a higher-tier priest rather than a fixed service price list.

After Blackstone Temple is reclaimed, several congregations debate stewardship of the larger site. That discussion is an early example of Bellweather having to decide whether reclamation means restoration of old ownership, new public use, or shared control.

entries.name: How to Use This Chapter
entries: This is the recurring campaign hub. Use it between expeditions rather than as a single linear adventure. After every major chapter, show one visible improvement in Bellweather and one new tension created by recovery.

entries.name: Ledger House Between Expeditions
entries: Ledger House is the campaign’s emotional anchor and a reliable source of street-level information.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Use ordinary patrons to tell the party what changed because of their last mission.
Let rumors from the chapter’s existing tables surface naturally through workers, merchants, guards, refugees, and travelers.
Give the party room to rest, plan, and disagree without an urgent clock unless the next chapter specifically creates one.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Brakkus offers information and shelter, not orders. He is most useful when the characters ask who is affected, who is hiring, or what happened while they were gone.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: Brakkus hears practical rumors but should not know hidden villain plans.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Relationships made here can provide later testimony, shelter, supplies, or political support.

entries.name: The Council Hall
entries: The Council handles public contracts, petitions, payments, property claims, and security.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Wern Ursen focuses on defense and civilian safety. Bishop Brann focuses on refugees, burial rights, and religious sites. Perrin Cardon argues that restored property and commerce are necessary for Bellweather to survive.
When the party brings evidence, the Council can authorize guards, funds, legal access, or investigations. Bureaucracy takes time and creates records.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Perrin begins as competent and useful, not sinister. Wern, a dwarf, respects direct plans. Bishop Brann asks who bears the cost of a decision.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: Official decisions leave paper trails that become important during Perrin’s later betrayal.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Council support can make an expedition easier, but seeking it is always optional.

entries.name: Markets and Downtime
entries: Bellweather should feel more alive after each successful reclamation.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Add reopened stalls, workshops, inns, shrines, and construction crews as routes become safe.
Allow training, research, shopping, carousing, crafting, or faction work between missions.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Downtime spent helping a faction can improve its attitude or create a useful contact.

entries.name: City Change
entries: At the end of each expedition, choose one improvement and one tension tied directly to what was reclaimed.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Improvements include reopened streets, repaired wells, restored shrines, safer river traffic, new housing, or new markets.
Tensions include rent increases, competing deeds, displaced squatters, private guards, tax disputes, labor shortages, or arguments about who paid the risk of reclamation.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: The city never resets. Later chapters should refer back to earlier decisions whenever practical.

entries.name: Rewards
entries: These rewards are party totals for the campaign's four-character party.

items: {@b Spendable wealth.} No automatic chapter payout.
{@b Consumables.} Purchased normally through available markets.
{@b Permanent magic.} None automatically.
{@b Story reward.} Downtime, shopping, favors, faction access, and the benefits of a growing Bellweather.

data.name: Chapter 3: The Slums
entries: {@b Recommended level:} 3–4

entries.name: Open in the 5etools Dynamic Map Viewer
entries: Clicking the map image itself opens the source image. To use 5etools' zoomable interactive map viewer instead, open the {@link DM Screen|dmscreen.html}.

In the DM Screen, add a panel and choose {@b Adventure/Book Map Dynamic Viewer}. Select {@b No Cause for Alarm: Ruins of Bellweather}, then {@b Chapter 3: The Slums}, then {@b The Slums — DM Tactical Map}. The viewer provides zoom and pan controls and uses the keyed map regions A1, B2, C3, D4, E4, and E5.
Use the matching Player Tactical Map when you want the same geometry without DM-only keyed labels.

entries.name: Chapter Overview
entries: {@b Chapter purpose.} Secure a practical corridor through the Slums while establishing that reclamation involves people, property, and competing claims.
The party enters the Slums to locate a missing survey crew and establish a usable route through the district.
Their success opens the first reliable route into the ruins and gives Bellweather confidence to attempt more ambitious reclamation.
{@b Leads onward.} Petitions from residents and clergy report that armed militants have fortified Blackstone Temple and are holding caretakers inside.

entries.name: Running the Chapter
entries: {@b Primary objectives.} Rescue the survey crew, identify actual threats, establish safe routes, decide how squatters and residents are treated.
{@b Player agency.} A second route into the district, negotiation with unaffiliated residents, or direct clearing are all valid.
{@b Fail forward.} The survey crew can always be found; failures mean injury, lost equipment, or hostile attention.

{@b Rest and pressure.} Safe long rests are available back at Ledger House. Inside the active adventure site, resting gives opposing factions time to reposition unless the characters secure a defensible refuge.

entries.name: Opening Route Through the Slums
entries: After the storm and Ledger House, Brakkus points out several ways capable people can find work. Council reclamation is the official route, but a private survey crew, residents, merchants, or simple exploration can all pull the party toward the Slums. Run {@b 2–3 meaningful encounters}, not a block-by-block extermination. {@b Suggested opening sequence:} first, a mixed scavenger crew searching an abandoned shop, with one scavenger carrying a bundle of brass fittings and door hardware. Treat this primarily as a social and choice encounter; negotiation, intimidation, observation, retreat, or combat are all valid, and the scavengers should not attack simply because the party approaches. Second, route the party through a collapsed residence where a hungry {@creature Grick|XMM} provides the reliable combat beat for the session. This combat should occur before the party reaches the survey crew even if the scavengers are resolved peacefully. If time remains, reveal the trail toward the missing survey crew and end on that clue. Save the giant-spider warehouse encounter and the survey-crew rescue for later in the chapter. Negotiation, retreat, and cooperation remain valid outcomes whenever the opposition is intelligent and not committed to violence.
{@i Map of the Slums.}

The Slums are the first reclamation district and should begin after the storm and Ledger House scenes. The source describes this district as former lower- and middle-class housing now serving as a buffer between the reclaimed quarter and hostile-held parts of the old city. That social history is important: these are homes and workshops that became dangerous after Bellweather fell, not a neighborhood whose residents are inherently lesser.

The Council's assignment is simple: push the safe line outward, identify structures that can be occupied, rescue people in danger, and neutralize immediate threats. The party does not have to kill every creature in the district. Negotiated departures, alliances, surrender, and identifying harmless residents all count toward reclamation.

entries.name: The Survey Crew Rescue
entries: Use one early encounter to establish the personal cost of reclamation. A small mixed-species Bellweather survey crew has been sent beyond the safest cleared line to mark property boundaries and structural hazards. A collapse or territorial creature has trapped one worker while another is injured.

The workers are ordinary people. They do not become recurring plot devices unless the players take an interest in them. Their presence simply establishes that the Council's maps, deeds, and recovery plans depend on people doing dangerous work before a district is safe.

Afterward, a worker can ask a practical question such as, {@b “Do they already know who gets these buildings?”} Do not turn it into a speech; let the question sit beside the visible fact that reclamation creates both safety and valuable property.

entries.name: Optional Jarrock Thread: Rena Dask
entries: Rena Dask, a dwarf stonemason and informal crew representative, can be part of the survey/reclamation workforce without changing the encounter roster or map. She helps stabilize the injured and immediately returns to practical work.

If Jarrock engages her, Rena asks a simple question rather than making a speech: {@b "When we make one of these buildings safe enough to own again, who gets paid for making it worth owning?"} Let the answer remain unresolved for now.

{@b Keyed-area encounters.} When a scene and a keyed location describe the same encounter, use the roster and objective in the scene. Creatures listed only in the keyed reference apply when the characters explore that location outside the scene sequence.

entries.name: A1 — Boundary Crossing / Scavenger Position
entries: The controlled crossing from secured Bellweather into the Slums. Four bandits watch the ruined storefront here and attempt to collect a street toll; negotiation, intimidation, retreat, or combat are all valid outcomes.

entries.name: B2 — Residents / Mera Kest Area
entries: Partially occupied homes nearest the frontier. Mera Kest and nearby residents can provide local information, including the survey crew's route toward the old dye works and reports of movement near the collapsed warehouse.

entries.name: C3 — Collapsed Residence
entries: The collapsed residence used for the opening combat beat. Broken masonry, unstable flooring, and a hungry grick make this the first unavoidable predatory threat on the route deeper into the neighborhood.

entries.name: D4 — Predator / Hazard Zone
entries: Unstable rubble and broken structures between the warehouse and dye works. Use this area for the grick's approach, environmental pressure, or a bypass route; it does not require an additional combat if the existing scene roster is already sufficient.

entries.name: E4 — Old Dye Works
entries: The industrial ruin that anchors Scene 3. Its vats, broken work areas, and adjoining rubble form the final approach to the missing survey crew.

entries.name: E5 — Missing Survey Crew Site
entries: Lessa Dorn and Kav Orin are barricaded here. Rescuing them establishes the practical corridor Bellweather can secure after the chapter. Their survey field satchel contains 2 Potions of Healing carried as emergency medical supplies. The satchel can be recovered even if the rescue goes badly or one or more surveyors die.

entries.name: Location and Background Details
entries: The Slum District was once a neighborhood of lower- and middle-class dwellings. Since Bellweather established the Reclaimed Quarter, this district has become a dangerous buffer between settled streets and territories controlled by scattered factions, predators, squatters, and desperate scavengers. The Slums are the next section targeted for reclamation, and some residents have already begun repairing homes and shops nearest the gate. No single ancestry or species defines the opposition here. Some inhabitants are hostile, some frightened, some opportunistic, and some simply trying to survive. Use the {@b Unaligned Ruin District} encounters in Appendix A.

entries.name: Scene 1: Entering the District
entries: {@b Map areas:} {@area A1 — Boundary Crossing|3a1|x} and {@area B2 — Residents / Mera Kest Area|3b2|x}. Begin at A1; B2 holds the nearby residents and local information that points deeper into the district.
The Slums are inhabited ruins, not an empty dungeon. The first challenge is determining who is dangerous and who is merely trying to live there.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Use the Player Map for navigation and the DM Keyed Map for encounter locations.

Four scavengers pick through a ruined storefront and the rubble around it; use {@creature Bandit|XMM|Bandit} stat blocks if combat breaks out. One carries a club, one carries a bundle of brass fittings and door hardware, and two keep salvaged items partly hidden behind their backs. They are wary and defensive but do not attack first. They prefer talking, bluffing, bargaining, or backing away to a fight.
Nearby residents watch how the characters respond.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Mera Kest, a human woman, speaks for the bandits. She is greedy rather than loyal to a cause and bargains if outmatched. Residents answer questions if treated as residents rather than suspects.

entries.name: Encounter
entries: 4 scavengers (use {@creature Bandit|XMM|Bandit} stat blocks). They fight only if threatened, attacked, cornered, or convinced the party intends to rob or arrest them. If combat begins, they flee or surrender when two are incapacitated or when an escape route opens.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: Mera saw the missing survey crew head toward the old dye works. She has heard clicking in the rafters near a collapsed warehouse.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Killing surrendering bandits harms local goodwill. Driving them off or bargaining leaves witnesses who may help later.

entries.name: Scene 2: Collapsed Residence
entries: {@b Map areas:} {@area C3 — Collapsed Residence|3c3|x} and {@area D4 — Predator / Hazard Zone|3d4|x}. Run the grick encounter at C3 as the opening reliable combat beat. D4 is adjoining rubble on the route toward the dye works and foreshadows the deeper danger without adding another mandatory fight.
The route deeper into the district passes through a collapsed residence where a hungry grick has learned to ambush anything moving through the rubble.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Broken masonry and fallen furniture create patches of difficult terrain. A character who studies the rubble spots signs of a lurking predator without a roll; otherwise use DC 13 Wisdom (Perception) to notice the grick before it attacks.

entries.name: Encounter
entries: 1 {@creature Grick|XMM}. It is hungry, territorial, and not interested in negotiation. If the party is badly depleted from the storm, it begins in a poor position rather than gaining surprise.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: A dead scavenger carries survey ribbon. Drag marks show at least two surveyors left the warehouse alive.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Destroying the nest makes this route safe for later labor crews.

entries.name: Scene 3: The Dye Works
entries: {@b Map areas:} {@area D4 — Predator / Hazard Zone|3d4|x}, {@area E4 — Old Dye Works|3e4|x}, and {@area E5 — Missing Survey Crew Site|3e5|x}. Beyond this point, webbing and movement around D4 lead toward the dye works, where Lessa Dorn and Kav Orin are barricaded at E5.
Two surveyors are barricaded inside while giant spiders hunt through the adjoining rubble and damaged structures.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: The survivors, Lessa Dorn, a half-elf woman, and Kav Orin, a halfling man, are exhausted and nearly out of water. Their third member, Harl, a human man, left to seek help. Their field satchel contains 2 Potions of Healing carried as emergency medical supplies; the party can recover it regardless of the rescue outcome.

{@b NPC description — Lessa Dorn and Kav Orin.} Lessa is a lean half-elf woman in early middle age, sun-browned and visibly angry beneath a layer of dust, with a torn survey coat and a measuring cord still looped at her belt. Kav is a younger halfling man, compact and hollow-eyed from exhaustion, who keeps glancing toward exits as if expecting another attack. Both carry the practical gear of people who spend more time in ruins than offices.
The {@creature Giant Spider|XMM|Giant Spiders} use webbing and ruined walls to cut off the safest approach to the trapped surveyors.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Lessa is angry about inadequate protection. Kav wants to leave immediately. Both become useful witnesses if treated well.

entries.name: Encounter
entries: 2 {@creature Giant Spider|XMM|Giant Spiders}; use 1 if the party enters this encounter badly depleted or has not had a safe rest.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: The survey crew found chalk marks used by bandits and a newer symbol—three vertical cuts crossed by a diagonal line—on crates that did not belong to them.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: The surveyors can guide Bellweather workers through the district once rescued.

entries.name: Scene 4: Harl and the Lost Strongbox
entries: {@b Map placement:} Place Harl and the strongbox in the rubble between {@area D4|3d4|x} and {@area E4|3e4|x}; no additional map key is required.
Harl lies pinned beneath a fallen beam near Jorn Milar’s storm-lost strongbox.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: Taking ten minutes and using leverage frees Harl automatically. Under pressure, DC 12 Strength (Athletics) frees him quickly.
The strongbox contains 40 gp and mundane trade papers.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Harl is embarrassed that he left the others but did so to seek help, not abandon them.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: Harl saw armed strangers carrying supply crates deeper east. They were not the local bandits.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: Returning the strongbox earns Jorn’s promised payment. Saving Harl earns worker goodwill.

entries.name: Scene 5: Return to Bellweather
entries: The party returns with rescued surveyors, a reopened route, and evidence that someone is supplying multiple groups.

entries.name: What Happens
entries: The Council honors any contract. Residents ask whether reopening the district means eviction. Perrin congratulates the party and notes that safe roads make every other recovery possible.

entries.name: NPC Behavior
entries: Perrin should sound reasonable; he is not yet a villain in presentation.

entries.name: Clues and Discoveries
entries: The recurring crossed-line symbol becomes the campaign’s first indication of coordination.

entries.name: Consequences
entries: The characters remain level 3 through Blackstone Temple. If using milestones, advance them to level 4 after Blackstone Temple is resolved. Blackstone Temple becomes the next major problem along the reopened route.

entries.name: Transition to Chapter 4
entries: Petitions from residents and clergy report that armed militants have fortified Blackstone Temple and are holding caretakers inside.

In adventure outcome, the transition also centers on the missing survey crew: Blackstone militants knowingly kidnapped the two surviving surveyors. The Council wants them recovered, while Bishop Brann wants the detained temple caretakers rescued and sacred records preserved.

entries.name: Rewards
entries: {@b Treasure and rewards.} The posted reclamation contract pays {@b 75 gp per character} on completion (300 gp for a four-character party). During the expedition, place roughly {@b 200–250 gp} of additional party value in recoverable coin, jewelry, trade goods, legitimate salvage, and private recovery bonuses. The strongbox and similar identifiable property are not free salvage: returning them earns the stated private reward. The survey crew's field satchel at E5 contains 2 Potions of Healing as emergency medical supplies, and the satchel remains recoverable even if the rescue goes badly. Award one useful uncommon consumable such as Dust of Disappearance only if the party explores a sealed workshop; otherwise use mundane salvage.

entries.name: Slums Aftermath
entries: {@b Level progression.} The party remained 3rd level through the Slums and advanced only after Blackstone Temple was resolved.

{@b Route into the Slums.} Jord’s missing strongbox drew the party into the district. Aaron and Jarrock followed tracks from Jord’s wagon, Pepper learned from Tiera Dame at The Tiny Mage that theft was common in the Slums, and Arumen entered the district independently.

{@b Tiera Dame.} A compact halfling woman with quick dark eyes, a practical apron over mismatched traveling clothes, and several small pouches tied at her belt. She talks rapidly, watches customers’ hands as much as their faces, and gives the impression that very little happens in the Slums without eventually reaching her ears.

{@b Jord.} A road-worn gnome merchant in his middle years, broad through the shoulders and dressed for travel rather than display. His coat is good quality but dusty, his hands are callused from handling cargo, and he speaks with the brisk courtesy of someone used to bargaining without wasting time.

{@b Mara.} Pepper initiated violence during the scavenger confrontation. Two scavengers were killed, two escaped, and Mara was intimidated into revealing activity near the grick house before fleeing. Mara remains a recurring Slums NPC.

{@b Kaleb.} The party found Council surveyor Kaleb unconscious in the dye house. Pepper killed him with a mace, took his marked survey satchel and tools, and the party buried the body inside the building. A Slums gate guard later recognized the marked satchel, making clear that Kaleb had been one of the missing Council surveyors rather than an enemy combatant.
{@b The remaining surveyors.} Kaleb’s crew had three members. The other two, Lessa Dorn and Kav Orin, were abducted by the Blackstone faction and held with the temple caretakers.
{@b Aaron.} Ledger House feels familiar to Aaron because of recurring dreams. Advance this thread when Aaron chooses to investigate the connection.
{@b Pepper.} Pepper reached Bellweather while searching for the Library of Alexandria. Brakkus has heard only vague rumors of an old library deeper in the ruins.
{@b Arumen.} Arumen does not know how they arrived in Bellweather; they were teleported there, and the cause remains unexplained.

data.name: Chapter 4: Blackstone Temple
entries: {@b Recommended level:} 4. Adventure note: this four-character party completed Blackstone at level 3 and advances to level 4 before Kellan’s Well.

entries.name: Chapter Overview
entries: {@b Adventure status.} Blackstone Temple is resolved. The four level-3 PCs freed the seven captives, killed Tal Rusk and his remaining guards, recovered the reliquary, and returned it to Bishop Brann.
The Council now holds Tal’s coded ledger, the spyglass, and the compass. Pepper’s Kaleb investigation has produced a five-mission sentence and Ledger House arrest under Brakkus’s supervision.
{@b Leads onward.} Everyone accepted Kellan’s Well. The chapter begins the next morning after a long rest and level-up with four level-4 PCs.

entries.name: Running the Chapter
entries: {@b First conversation.} Let Nela and the other captives explain the ledger, the altar maintenance passage, and the orders to remove Bishop Brann’s sacred material. Lessa and Kav can identify themselves as the two surviving members of Kaleb’s survey crew and do not yet know Kaleb is dead.
{@b Tal next.} Tal Rusk and four Guards are the remaining organized interior force. Tal’s primary goal is the coded ledger Pepper holds. Negotiation is a fully valid resolution.
{@b Coded ledger.} The coded ledger is the key Iron Covenant document at the center of the Blackstone standoff.
{@b Civilians remain separate.} Dependents, coerced refugees, temple caretakers, surveyors, and ordinary residents are not enemy combatants.

{@b Rest and pressure.} Safe long rests remain available at Ledger House. If the party withdraws from the active temple before resolving Tal, Tal can reposition, evacuate, or prepare defenses based on what he knows.

entries.name: Scene 1: The Seven Captives
entries: {@b Nela Orr.} Older human woman; soot-stained gray temple robes; cropped silver hair; firm, controlled voice. Before being recaptured, Nela briefly escaped, stole Tal Rusk’s coded Iron Covenant ledger, locked and hid it in the safe, and returned to captivity under guard.

{@b What Nela knows.} She knows the maintenance passage behind the altar, overheard orders to pack and remove Bishop Brann’s sacred records and relics, and knows Tal badly wants the coded ledger returned.
{@b Dwarf caretaker.} Middle-aged, shaved head, ink-stained fingers; exhausted but focused on preserving the temple records.
{@b Halfling caretaker.} Young, bruised face, torn vestments; frightened but mobile.
{@b Half-orc caretaker.} Broad-shouldered, one arm in a sling; protective of the other captives.
{@b Temple guard.} Human, battered mail, bandaged thigh, pale from blood loss but alert. The guard can describe interior movement and confirm Tal still has four Guards.
{@b Lessa Dorn.} Lean, weathered half-elf Council surveyor. She knows the Iron Covenant abducted the survey crew but does not know Kaleb is dead.
{@b Kav Orin.} Halfling Council surveyor. He knows the Iron Covenant abducted the survey crew but does not know Kaleb is dead.
{@b Kaleb.} Do not use a satchel-recognition trigger. Lessa and Kav can naturally ask whether the party found Kaleb once introductions establish that the characters came through the Slums.
{@b Nela’s motive.} She will not willingly abandon another captive and prioritizes getting everyone safe while keeping the temple’s sacred material from the Covenant.
{@b Lessa’s play cue.} She is angry that the survey crew was sent into danger with inadequate protection; she still does not know Kaleb is dead.
{@b Kav’s play cue.} He wants out of Blackstone alive.

entries.name: Scene 2: Tal Rusk and the Ledger
entries: {@b Tal Rusk.} A compact, scarred dwarf in practical heavy armor, controlled rather than theatrical. He commands four Guards deeper inside Blackstone and is the remaining Iron Covenant commander on site.

{@b His objective.} Tal’s highest priority is recovering the coded Iron Covenant ledger Pepper holds. He cares more about protecting Covenant intelligence, contacts, and supply information than about dying for the temple.

{@b Tal’s play cue.} Controlled, professional, and not suicidal. He intimidates first, but his real priority is recovering the ledger and preserving Covenant intelligence; he negotiates when that serves those goals better than combat.

{@b The bargain.} In exchange for the ledger, Tal can order himself and his four remaining Guards to withdraw from Blackstone. The seven captives remain free, and Bishop Brann’s sacred records and relics remain intact. The escaped gate captain and Guard are already gone and are not part of the bargain.

{@b If the party keeps the ledger.} Tal will not voluntarily abandon the temple while the ledger remains in the party’s hands. If negotiation fails, run {@creature Tal Rusk|NCFA} and 4 {@creature Guard|XMM|Guards} as the decisive Blackstone combat. Tal can surrender or order a retreat if defeated; his force is not suicidal.

{@b If the ledger is returned.} Tal withdraws with his four Guards. The party gives up the coded intelligence unless it was copied or decoded first, but they keep the rescued captives and recover Bishop Brann’s sacred material.

entries.name: Scene 3: Return to Ledger House and the Council
entries: After Blackstone is resolved, Lessa Dorn and Kav Orin report what happened. A Council envoy requires a meeting at Ledger House. A character deliberately listening to the envoy’s private exchange with Brakkus can make a DC 20 Perception check to overhear it.
The Council participants are Ulric Evern, Wern Ursen, Bishop Brann, and Perrin Cardon. Reclamation crews have now searched the Slums and found Kaleb’s body with his head smashed.

entries.name: Council NPC Play Cues
entries: {@b Brakkus.} Protect the people under his roof; stay calm, dry, practical, and restrained. He does not exist to steer the party’s decisions.
{@b Ulric Evern.} Budget hawk and hard bargainer; press for accountability and a consequence Bellweather can actually enforce.
{@b Wern Ursen.} Defense and infrastructure; frame the issue around security, operational risk, and whether the party can still be useful safely.
{@b Bishop Brann.} Public welfare, healing, burial rights, preservation of sacred records, and humane treatment of prisoners.
{@b Perrin Cardon.} Polished and ambitious; values useful routes and the political value of keeping effective adventurers working. Do not play him as an exposed villain.
{@b Council envoy.} Procedural messenger only.

Brakkus may tell the envoy that Pepper killed Kaleb if he knows that fact. The Council then questions the party, but there is no scripted confession or predetermined evidentiary outcome; play the scene from what the characters say and what the Council can establish.

{@b Pepper consequence.} If the Council establishes that Pepper murdered Kaleb, Pepper must complete five mandatory Council missions total: the first is unpaid and the next four are paid normally. Refusal or abandonment of the required service means jail. This sentence applies to Pepper, not automatically to the rest of the party.

{@b Later emotional beat.} Kaleb’s wife can later confront Pepper at Ledger House while seeking help for her ill daughter. The daughter’s condition can be cured by Greater Restoration. Helping is Pepper’s choice and is not part of the sentence.

entries.name: Transition to Chapter 5
entries: All four characters have already agreed to Kellan’s Well. The Council’s reason to act is independent of the ledger: separate armed groups use coordinated signals and routes there, and the catacombs/waterworks are strategically important.
Kellan’s Well is the first of Pepper’s five mandatory Council missions and is unpaid for Pepper. Her remaining four required missions are paid normally. Refusal or abandonment means jail.
Blackstone Temple ended as the party entered Ledger House. The chapter begins the next morning after a long rest and level-up, with four level-4 PCs.

entries.name: Rewards
entries: {@b Actual reward.} Tal had 50 gp, his weapons, and the reliquary. Pepper kept Tal’s weapons; the party received the 50 gp.
{@b Bishop Brann.} The party returned the reliquary to him. He paid 300 gp total to the party, which they split, and gave Arunem Oil of Slipperiness.
{@b Temple find.} Arunem found a Scroll of Lesser Restoration.
{@b Council custody.} The coded ledger, spyglass, and compass are now Council evidence rather than party inventory.

{@link Interior Command — Tal Rusk + 4 Guards|https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sefjoe/no-cause-for-alarm-5etools/main/encounters/blackstone-interior-response.json}
The front-court, side-wall, and drainage presets are alternate approach material and should not be inserted into Blackstone Temple.

data.name: Chapter 5: Delving into Kellan's Well
entries: {@b Recommended level:} 4.

entries.name: ACTUAL PLAY OVERRIDE — October 11 Session, Read First
entries: THIS CHAPTER IS ALREADY PLAYED. The previous preparation to repair or reactivate the main sluice was explicitly removed from campaign continuity after the session. The party's mission is complete upon clearing the Iron Covenant; they have NO outstanding sluice task, and the current state of waterworks restoration is not a campaign requirement. The mechanical details of the sluice deeper in this chapter are historical unplayed reference, not an unfinished quest.

Actual table: the alarm was not raised, three Bow Gallery Scouts were present/encountered, Arunem broke through the ceiling to flank Noren and his Warrior Veteran, and the party captured and tied both. The Decanter of Endless Water was found and passed to Pepper. Session 4 resumes WITHIN THE WATERWORKS DURING THE PARTY'S SHORT REST, with both prisoners alive and bound. Their fate is still undecided.

Do not retroactively add a fourth Scout, a missed sluice objective, a required skill check to restore flow, or an additional Council errand to release the party. Bishop Brann can deliver the already-agreed 300 gp compensation for completion. The old sluice-scene map/mechanics can remain for reference only if the PCs voluntarily revisit them.
