data.name: Appendix H: Design Notes for Grayson
entries: I want to write this down because by the time we finish this campaign, there are going to be things I forget. Not the big stuff. I will probably remember Pepper killing Kaleb forever. What I am more likely to forget are the weird little turns along the way: the names that changed, the adventures I almost used, the ideas I was convinced were going to be important and then threw away, and the things you guys did at the table that made me rewrite what I thought the campaign was going to be.
So this is not the story of what happened {@i in} No Cause for Alarm. This is the story of how I built it, how I kept changing it, and how you and the other players changed it with me.

entries.name: The First Version: Osric and the Silent Vault
entries: The oldest version of this campaign looked almost nothing like the version you are playing now.

The earliest character at the center of it was named {@b Osric}. Most of my notes from this part are gone, which is annoying because I would really like to be able to show you exactly what I was thinking. What I do remember clearly is that Osric eventually became {@b Milton Foal}. They were not two different characters. Milton was what Osric turned into as I kept working on the idea.

The big location was the {@b Silent Vault}. The Vault was supposed to be an old containment facility with increasingly severe magical protections the deeper you went. At some point, the idea became that magic itself would be suppressed in the lower parts.

You were supposed to go into the Vault to rescue {@b Tomas Reed}. Milton had been trapped there for an absurd amount of time. The later version had him connected to someone named {@b Malthivar}, and Milton had one really stupid-looking but important possession: Malthivar's old staff had somehow been reduced to an ordinary broom.
I liked that. Not because the broom was secretly going to turn back into the Staff of Ultimate Ass-Kicking or something. It mattered because Milton cared about it.
That is something I still like in NCFA now. An object does not need a stat block to matter. Sometimes an old broom is important because it is the last thing somebody has from another life.

The plan for the Vault eventually involved its containment systems failing or being triggered while the party was rescuing Tomas. You would get Tomas out. You would also free Milton. And freeing Milton was supposed to cause much bigger problems later.

entries.name: What Milton Was Supposed to Become
entries: Milton was not supposed to show up with a sign over his head that said VILLAIN.
The thing that defined him was {@b freedom}. After being trapped and controlled for so long, freedom had become basically sacred to him.
At first, that is easy to sympathize with. People should be free. Okay.
Then it starts moving a little. People need enough power to protect their freedom. Still pretty reasonable.
Then: If people cannot protect themselves, maybe somebody stronger needs to protect them. Now we are getting into dangerous territory.
And eventually: If people make choices that threaten their own freedom, maybe somebody else should make those choices for them.

That was where Milton was headed. I liked the idea that he could become a villain without ever abandoning his original belief. He would still tell you that everything he was doing was about freedom. He would just gradually redefine freedom until it meant Milton deciding what is best for everybody else.

That idea did not disappear when Milton stopped being the main villain. There is still a lot of that DNA in NCFA: power, control, the excuses people make when they think they know better than everyone else, and the difference between helping someone and deciding for them.

entries.name: I Knew the Kind of Campaign I Wanted Before I Knew the Campaign
entries: Even back then, there were some things I knew I wanted.
I wanted you guys to have a place that felt like home. I wanted you to be able to leave, go do something dangerous, and come back.

I wanted that home to change. If you saved a neighborhood, I wanted people to move back into it. If a road became safe, I wanted merchants to start using it. If trade came back, I wanted money to start moving around. If money started moving around, I wanted somebody to get rich and somebody else to get pissed off.

I wanted the world to keep going while you were somewhere else. While you are in a dungeon, somebody is fixing a roof. Somebody is going to work. Somebody is putting their kid to bed. Somebody is getting into a bar fight. Somebody is cheating at cards. Somebody is having a really boring day. Most of those things will never become adventures. They are still happening.
That is one of the biggest things I want NCFA to feel like: {@b You are the center of the story. You are not the center of the world.}

If every weird thing in Bellwether turns out to be Tyren, the world gets smaller. If every old ruin is connected to Perrin, the world gets smaller. If every criminal is secretly part of the Iron Covenant, the world gets smaller. Sometimes a criminal is just a criminal. Sometimes two guys get drunk and fight. Sometimes a library is just a library.

That is why I decided not to turn the library into something like the Library of Alexandria. It did not need to secretly be one of the most important libraries that ever existed. It could just be important to Bellwether. That is enough.

entries.name: Looking for an Old Adventure That Already Did What I Wanted
entries: At some point I realized I was trying to solve a campaign-structure problem that D&D had probably solved before.
This was going to be my first long campaign as a DM. I did not see any particular virtue in making my job harder just so I could say I had invented every single thing myself.
So I started digging through published adventures.
The question was not: What published campaign should I run?
The question was: {@b Is there an old campaign whose structure already matches what I am trying to build?}
If there was, I could steal the useful bones and build NCFA on top of them.

entries.name: Under Illefarn
entries: One of the first serious possibilities was {@i Under Illefarn}.
There was a lot I liked about it. It was grounded. There was a community. There were older ruins beneath the current world. It worked at the lower levels where I wanted to start.
For a while I thought I might use it as the opening and then transition into something larger: use Under Illefarn to get everybody started, then move into the real long-term campaign structure.
I eventually dropped that. The more I changed the opening to fit what I wanted, the less reason there was to use Under Illefarn in the first place.
At some point you are no longer saving yourself work by adapting something. You are just doing extra work to make somebody else's story look like yours. That became a recurring lesson.

entries.name: Against the Slave Lords
entries: I looked at {@i Against the Slave Lords} too.

There were things in that series I liked a lot. You have local problems that turn out to be part of something larger. There is an organized enemy. You can investigate your way upward through a network. There is a real sense that somebody behind the scenes is benefiting from all of this.
The problem was that once you make the Slave Lords the campaign backbone, the campaign becomes about finding and stopping the Slave Lords. The villains become the spine.
I wanted the {@b city} to be the spine. Bellwether still needed to matter even during stretches when nobody was thinking about the main villain.
So I kept ideas from that kind of structure, but not the structure itself.

entries.name: The Bloodstone Adventures
entries: I also looked at the {@i Bloodstone} series.

That was attractive for almost the opposite reason. Those adventures get huge: settlements, armies, politics, territory, and high-level threats. The characters eventually become major figures in the world.

I liked that sense of escalation. I still do. I want there to be a point where you can look back and say: We used to care about one spider in a warehouse, and now look at the crap we are dealing with.
But Bloodstone starts too far up that ladder for what I wanted.
I wanted the small stuff to matter first. A warehouse should matter. A missing person should matter. Opening a road should matter. Helping one family should matter.
You guys should become important. You should not begin the campaign as people who already operate at the scale of armies and kingdoms.
So Bloodstone was interesting to look at, especially for what a campaign could become later, but it was not the right foundation.

entries.name: Princes of the Apocalypse
entries: {@i Princes of the Apocalypse} was probably one of the more serious possibilities.
It had multiple factions. It had different directions you could go. It was less like following one hallway from Chapter 1 to Chapter 2 to Chapter 3. I liked that.
For a while, I could imagine using that kind of regional structure and then replacing pieces with my own material.
The problem was eventually obvious. If I used Princes of the Apocalypse as the backbone, NCFA would become the elemental cult campaign.
The cults would determine what mattered. The cult locations would determine where you went. The cult plot would determine the campaign's shape.

And I was getting more interested in Bellwether itself than I was in any particular enemy organization: who owns the rebuilt buildings, who gets rich when a district becomes safe, who gets pushed out, who controls the roads, what the Council does, what the churches do, and what ordinary people think.
Those questions mattered more to me than elemental temples. So that one went away too.

entries.name: The Anthology Books
entries: I also looked at adventures in books like {@i Candlekeep Mysteries}, {@i Journeys Through the Radiant Citadel}, and {@i Quests from the Infinite Staircase}.

Those were interesting for a different reason. I did not really think one of those books was going to be NCFA. But I thought I might be able to take individual adventures and drop them into the campaign.
Maybe one gave me a good mystery. Maybe one gave me a weird location. Maybe one gave me something I could use at a particular level.

That idea never completely went away. I still do not care where a good idea comes from. If an old adventure has a really good map, I can use the map. If it has a cool setup, I can steal the setup. If somebody wrote a great monster encounter forty years ago, there is no prize for pretending I did not see it.
The important thing is that once it comes into NCFA, it needs to feel like it belongs here. I never wanted it to feel like: Okay, this week we are visiting somebody else's campaign for three hours.

entries.name: Then I Found Ruins of Adventure
entries: Eventually I found {@i Ruins of Adventure}, the AD&D module connected to {@i Pool of Radiance}.
That one clicked almost immediately.

It had the thing I had been trying to build. A city had been mostly lost. A small part had been reclaimed. Beyond the safe area were dangerous districts. Adventurers could take jobs, push into those districts, deal with whatever was there, and gradually expand the part of the city that was usable again.
As the city was reclaimed, the situation changed.
That was basically the skeleton I had been looking for.
So this was the biggest early pivot in NCFA. I stopped trying to invent the entire campaign structure from zero and started using {@i Ruins of Adventure} as a {@b chassis}.
That word is important. Chassis. Not story. Not canon. Not a script. A chassis. It gave me a shape I could build on.

entries.name: The Loop I Really Wanted
entries: What I really took from Ruins of Adventure was the campaign loop:

items: You come home.
You see what changed.
You hear about several problems.
You pick something to do.
You leave the safe part of the city.
You do something dangerous.
You change the situation.
Then you come back.
And now home is a little different because of what you did.

entries: That is still one of the basic rhythms of NCFA.
Even now that the campaign has moved much farther away from Ruins of Adventure, I still really like that loop.
The city is not just the place where you buy potions between adventures. The city is part of the adventure.

entries.name: Bellwether Starts Replacing Phlan
entries: The more I worked on it, the less interested I became in simply converting Phlan.
Bellwether started becoming its own place.

The Council became its own thing. The neighborhoods started having their own problems. The factions became more specific. The politics became more specific. The reclamation started creating consequences that were not really part of the old module at all.
And then there was Ledger House.

entries.name: Where Brakkus Came From
entries: Brakkus was not created for NCFA.
You already knew that, but someday you might forget how much of him came from somewhere else.
{@b Brakkus Ledgerhelm was one of my characters at Hall of Heroes.}
I played him there every week for about four months, from around level 3 to level 10.
By the time I put him into this campaign, I had already spent a lot of hours being Brakkus.

That meant I knew him differently than I knew most NPCs. I knew how he reacted when somebody pissed him off. I knew when he would be patient. I knew when he would decide somebody was full of shit. I knew the things he took seriously. I knew the kind of humor he had. I knew what he thought a paladin was supposed to be.
That made him useful when I needed somebody to run the place that was supposed to feel like home.
But I had one big rule for myself: {@b Brakkus could not still be the hero.}
He had been my player character. Now I was the DM. This was not going to become a campaign where my old character follows you guys around being cooler than everybody. That would suck.
So I changed him.

entries.name: Turning My Character Into Your NPC
entries: The Brakkus you know at Ledger House is an older version of the Brakkus I played.
I did not throw away his Hall of Heroes history. I treated it like the earlier part of his life.
He adventured. He got older. He got much more powerful. And eventually, he stopped.
By NCFA, he is around forty-eight, a retired Oath of Devotion paladin of Torm, and the owner of Ledger House.

I expanded his history to fit that older version. His mother became Elena, a captive librarian in the Ironfang Clan. His father became Korgak, the warlord. After Elena died, Brakkus rejected his father's legacy and took the name Ledgerhelm in honor of his mother. He eventually trained under High Justiciar Vance Halford. Vance gave him the sword Brakkus named The Appendix.
A lot of that helped me answer the question: How did the adventurer I played become this guy behind the bar?
But the most important change was his job in the story.
At Hall, Brakkus was one of the protagonists. In NCFA, he is not.

He can be stronger than you. He can know things you do not know. He can have friends in places you have never been. If somebody comes into Ledger House looking to hurt people, they may discover that retirement does not mean helplessness.
But Brakkus is not supposed to go solve the campaign for you.
He gives you a home. He gives me a character I already understand. And then he gets out of the way.
{@b Brakkus was mine first. Bellwether is yours.}

entries.name: Then You Brought Me Jarrock
entries: Jarrock is probably the most interesting example of one of your ideas changing what I was building.
You did not make Jarrock for NCFA. You brought him in from {@b Jill's backstory}. Jill was already one of your characters from your Outschool campaign.
The strange thing about that was that we already knew something important about Jarrock's future.
Chronologically, that future has not happened yet. The Jarrock you are playing in NCFA is younger than the Jarrock from Jill's backstory.
But we already know that one day Jarrock kills Jill's parents, the King and Queen, and then takes Jill in.
That gave me a really interesting problem.
I did not want that future to happen just because somebody had written: Jarrock kills the King and Queen and takes Jill.
I wanted it to make sense.
I wanted us to someday be able to look at the Jarrock you are playing now and say: Yeah. I can see how that guy became the guy who did that.
There are two completely different parts to that. Why does Jarrock eventually kill the King and Queen? And why does the guy who just killed their parents take their kid home with him?
Those both need an answer.

entries.name: Jarrock Helped Create One of the Big Themes of NCFA
entries: This is where the theme of {@b power corrupting people} really started becoming important to me.
Not in the stupid version where anyone who becomes king automatically turns evil. That is too easy.
What interests me is what happens when someone gets enough power that fewer and fewer people can tell them no.

They start making exceptions for themselves. They start believing they understand things better than everybody else. They start thinking: Normally this would be wrong, but this situation is different.
Then: Normally nobody should have this authority, but I can be trusted with it.
Then eventually: I am the only one who can make this decision.
That is much more interesting to me.
And it gives Jarrock's future somewhere to come from.
At some point, Jarrock is apparently going to decide that removing the King and Queen from power is not enough. They need to be removed from existence.
That is a pretty extreme decision.
I do not want to just hand you the reason. I want Jarrock to live through things that make that future possible.

Maybe he sees people in power abuse it. Maybe he sees institutions protect the wrong person. Maybe he sees what happens when somebody who should have been stopped earlier is allowed to keep going. Maybe something completely different happens because of choices you make.
I do not know yet. That is the point.
I know where Jarrock eventually ends up. I do not know exactly how your Jarrock gets there. We get to find that out.

entries.name: And Then There Is Jill
entries: The other half of that story may be even more important.
Jarrock kills Jill's parents. Then he takes Jill in.
That tells me that somewhere in Jarrock's life he needs to develop a very strong distinction between what your parents did and who you are.
Jill did not choose his parents.
If the King and Queen eventually become people Jarrock thinks have to die, that does not make their son guilty.
That is something I want Jarrock to have the chance to discover through play.
Not through some stupid NPC who walks up to him and says: Hello, Jarrock. Today's moral lesson is that children are not responsible for their parents. That would be terrible.
I want the campaign to give him experiences. Then you decide what they mean to him.

If someday we reach Jill's story and Jarrock can look at that kid after killing his parents and think: They had to die. You did nothing wrong. Then the backstory will feel like something that actually grew out of his life.

entries.name: Jarrock Also Changed How I Run D&D
entries: Jarrock changed more than the story. He helped create one of my favorite house rules.
During the grick fight, Jarrock went down.
That made me think more about how being stabilized actually works at the table.
By the normal rules, once somebody is stable they can potentially spend a long time unconscious doing nothing. They are safe. But the player is sitting there watching everybody else play D&D.
I did not really like that.
So I came up with the rule we use now:
After you have been stabilized and have been down for three rounds, you can make a DC 15 Constitution check. If you succeed, you get back up with 1d4 hit points.
I like it. Three rounds is still a long time. DC 15 is not easy. 1d4 hit points is definitely not a full recovery. You can get punched right back down.
But at least the player has a chance to claw their way back into the fight.
That rule exists because of something that happened to your character.
That is the kind of thing I want these notes to remember. The players did not only change my plot. Sometimes you changed the rules of our table.

entries.name: Then We Actually Started Playing
entries: Once the campaign started, the version in my notes immediately stopped being the only version that mattered.
That is just how D&D works.
I can prepare five pages. You guys can spend fifteen minutes trying to climb the wrong wall. That actually happened.
Pepper and Arunem wandered off. You guys spent time on things I assumed would take thirty seconds. Combat took longer than I expected.
The scavengers taught me things. The spiders taught me things. The grick definitely taught me things.
The timing of that first session was already changing the way I thought about encounter design.
Then Pepper murdered Kaleb.

entries.name: Kaleb Was Not My Plot
entries: This is probably one of the clearest examples of how the players changed NCFA.
I did not sit down before Session 1 and think: I have a great long-term idea. Pepper is going to murder Kaleb, and then I can build an entire consequence arc out of it.
Pepper's player did that.
Once Kaleb was dead, though, I had to decide whether the world cared.
Of course it did.
Kaleb knew people. Kaleb had a wife. Kaleb had a daughter. The Council existed. There was a body.
The crime did not stop existing because the party left the room.
That one player decision created material I had never planned. And it is still creating material.

entries.name: Pepper Made Me Think Harder About Consequences
entries: The fun part is that Pepper has also been ridiculously lucky.
Things keep going Pepper's way. Evidence gets destroyed. Rolls work. The player started saying things like: I HAVE TO GET AWAY WITH THIS MURDER.
That made me want the consequences to be fair.
I do not want to just declare: Surprise, you're caught because the DM says so.

If Pepper gets exposed, I want it to happen because something in the world makes sense. Somebody knows something. Somebody survives. Some piece of evidence still exists. The Council starts connecting things.
Whatever it is, I want it to feel earned.
That eventually led to the idea that Pepper could be forced into Council service: one unpaid job and then a series of paid jobs, with jail hanging over the situation if Pepper refuses.
But there was another thing I cared about even more.
That punishment should not decide Pepper's morality.
That is why Kaleb's wife and daughter are separate.
At some point, I want Kaleb's wife to come to Ledger House furious. She can tell Pepper: You murdered my husband. And then, despite hating Pepper, she can need a cleric to help her daughter.
Pepper can help. Pepper can refuse.
I do not want helping them to be part of the sentence. I do not want the Council to order it. I do not want the player to get mechanical credit for doing the decent thing.
Because if Pepper helps, I want it to mean something. And if Pepper says: Fuck you and your kid, that means something too.
That entire story exists because of a thing somebody at the table did that I never planned.

entries.name: Blackstone Changed Too
entries: The same thing keeps happening.
At Blackstone, I could know who lived there. I could know who the captives were. I could know what the Iron Covenant was doing. I could prepare guards and rooms and clues.
Then you guys actually arrived.
You melted the bars off a rear window and went in that way.
Aaron killed a temple guard.
The guard captain got away. Another guard escaped too.
That matters. Somebody out there knows the party attacked Blackstone.
Pepper got the coded Iron Covenant ledger. You guys know Pepper has it.
Pepper had already taken the spyglass and compass from the satchel and burned the survey note.
Those choices changed the information state of the world.
The next session has to be based on the world that exists after you made those choices, not the world I had imagined before the session started.
That is increasingly how I think about campaign prep.

entries.name: The Council Stopped Being a Quest Board
entries: Originally, the Council was an easy way to hand out reclamation jobs.
That is useful. It still does that.
But once you guys actually started interacting with the city, the Council could not just be five NPCs waiting in a room until you came back for your next assignment.
It had to act too.

The Council can send surveyors. It can reclaim territory. It can investigate a body. It can make political decisions. It can be wrong. It can be useful. It can do something while you are somewhere else.
That is part of the living-world thing again.
If you ignore the Council for three sessions, the Council does not go into stasis. They keep being the Council.

entries.name: The Old Module Was Becoming Less and Less Important
entries: While all of this was happening, I was still technically using Ruins of Adventure as the big campaign framework.
But I kept changing it.

Different enemies. Different reasons for going places. Different clues. Different politics. Different rewards. Different NPCs. Different relationships. Sometimes completely different purposes for locations.
The more you guys played, the harder it became to justify saying: Well, this is what happens next because that is the next section in the old book.
Bellwether had its own momentum now.
The actual game was starting to tell me what should come next.
But I was still leaning on the published framework more than I really needed to.
Then I made Josric Pickle.

entries.name: Josric Pickle Changed NCFA Without Being in NCFA
entries: Josric is not part of this campaign.
But making {@i Josric Pickle's Practical Course for Adventurers} had a huge effect on how I thought about this campaign.
With Josric, I was building the adventure myself.
I was designing rooms. I was throwing ideas away. I was changing puzzles. I was thinking about pacing. I was asking what the players might try.
And I realized that I had developed a design rule I really liked:
{@b Give the players a problem. Do not give them the solution.}
I can know some ways a room might be solved. I should know how the room works. I should know what happens if you screw it up.
But I do not need to decide: The only correct solution is to do these four steps in this order.
If you guys come up with something better, great. That is D&D.
Josric made me realize that I trusted myself enough to build those situations without needing somebody else's adventure underneath them.
That was the real reason I pivoted NCFA back toward homebrew.

entries.name: The Question Changed
entries: Before Josric, I was still often thinking: How do I adapt the next part of Ruins of Adventure into Bellwether?
After Josric, the question became: {@b What should happen next in Bellwether?}
That sounds like a tiny difference. It is not.
One question assumes the old adventure is the roadmap and I am changing it.
The other assumes Bellwether is the roadmap and I can use the old adventure whenever it has something useful.
That is basically where Ruins of Adventure stopped being NCFA's spine.
It became a box of spare parts.
I can still steal from it. I probably will. But I no longer feel any obligation to follow it.
Josric is what gave me the confidence to make that change.

entries.name: Perrin Started Getting Better Once I Stopped Treating Him Like the Political Villain
entries: Perrin Cardon changed a lot too.
At first, he was more straightforward: old family, political ambitions, claims in the reclaimed city, money, influence.
He could become a political antagonist. That worked. But it was not especially deep.
Perrin got more interesting when I stopped treating these two things as opposites: Perrin really does want Bellwether rebuilt, and Perrin really does want power.
Both can be true.
He can help people. He can support reclamation. He can sincerely believe the Cardon family was wronged. He can think Bellwether needs stronger leadership.
And he can increasingly decide that the person who should have that authority is Perrin Cardon.
That is much more interesting to me.
He does not need to secretly hate the city.
His problem is that the thing he thinks is good for the city and the thing that is good for Perrin can become harder and harder for him to tell apart.

entries.name: Tyren Went Through an Even Bigger Change
entries: For a while, Tyren was basically a possessing intelligence behind the bigger supernatural plot.
That worked mechanically for the old campaign structure. But it always felt a little abstract.
The newer version finally gave him an identity I actually like.
Tyren is an {@b ancient emerald dragon who is imprisoned}.
That gives me a real answer for why somebody this powerful has to manipulate people instead of just doing everything himself.
He cannot.
So he needs people.
That immediately makes his relationship with Perrin more interesting.
Tyren did not create Perrin's ambition. He found it.
Perrin already had something Tyren could pull on.
That is how I want Tyren to work in general. He does not create everybody's flaws. He exploits what is already there.
That keeps him from becoming the explanation for the entire world.

entries.name: Tyren Is Not Secretly Responsible for Everything
entries: This is important enough that I want it written down.
Tyren did not make Pepper kill Kaleb.
Tyren did not create every corrupt person in Bellwether.
Tyren did not cause every tragedy.
Tyren does not need to secretly be behind the Iron Covenant, every crime, every politician and every bad decision.
The world was already messy.
People already wanted things. People already hurt each other. People already wanted money. People already wanted power.
Tyren is dangerous because he is very good at finding those things and using them.
He is an exploiter.
He is not the explanation for humanity.

entries.name: The Strange Problem Tyren Has With You Guys
entries: One of the things I really like about the new Tyren story is that the party is unusually difficult for him to influence.
Not because some prophecy says you are the Chosen Four. I do not really want that.
You are difficult for him because of who your characters already are.
Different people have different reasons. Some have trauma. Some have an unusually fixed sense of themselves. Some have moral convictions. Some just do not give Tyren the emotional handles he expects.
Brakkus has his own reasons. Bishop Brann has his own reasons.
The important part is that I do not want: Tyren can't control you because you're the protagonists.
I want: Tyren is starting to realize there is something unusual about these specific people.
That makes you important to him without making the entire universe revolve around you.

entries.name: I Also Do Not Want Tyren Playing Your Character for You
entries: Tyren can get through sometimes.
But I do not want his power to become: Hand me your character sheet for twenty minutes.
I hate that.
The model I like is closer to {@spell Command}.
One action.
One awful moment where something gets into your head and makes you do something.
Then you are you again.
It should be scary because it happened at all.
Not annoying because you stopped getting to play Jarrock.

entries.name: Jarrock's Future and the New Villain Structure Started Connecting Thematically
entries: This is where some of the newer ideas started lining up in a way I really like.
Not because they are secretly connected in the plot.
Because they are asking related questions.
Milton believed freedom could justify control.
Perrin believes his vision of restoration can justify more authority.
Tyren literally manipulates other people's will.
And sometime in Jarrock's future, Jarrock decides that a King and Queen have crossed a line where removing them from office is not enough.
These are different people in different situations.
But all of them let us keep poking at the same ugly question: {@b What happens when someone has too much power?}
And then the harder one: {@b What are you justified in doing about it?}
I am not building an answer for you. That would defeat the point.
I am building situations where Jarrock is going to have reasons to develop an answer of his own.

entries.name: What I Have Learned About Writing the Campaign
entries: At the beginning, I thought more in terms of plots.
Now I think much more in terms of situations.
Who is here? What do they want? What are they doing? What happens if nobody interferes?
Then you guys show up.
That is usually enough.
If I put the only important clue in one room and you never go into that room, I can move the information somewhere else if it makes sense.

Maybe somebody else knows it. Maybe it is in another document. Maybe you capture somebody. Maybe the place you decide to investigate turns out to contain the thing that moves the larger mystery forward.
I do not care whether you follow the route I imagined.
I care whether the world reacts honestly to the route you choose.
There is a difference between moving a clue and moving your choice.
I can move the clue.
I do not want to erase what you chose.

entries.name: You Guys Keep Writing Parts of the Campaign I Cannot Write
entries: There are things I can prepare.

I can invent Bellwether. I can decide what Perrin wants. I can decide what Tyren is doing. I can know what the Iron Covenant believes. I can build Kellan's Well. I can decide what the Council is arguing about.
What I cannot write is the part where four actual people sit down and start making decisions.
I did not write Pepper's murder.
I did not write Pepper's ridiculous luck afterward.
I did not write Aaron killing the temple guard.
I did not write the captain escaping.
I did not write Jarrock going down against the grick.
I did not write Pepper getting back up on a natural 20.
I did not write the fifteen minutes of screwing around with the wall.
Those are now part of NCFA anyway.
And they are not filler.
They change what I do next.
That means this campaign belongs to all of us in a way a novel never could.
I own the world behind the screen.
You guys own your characters.
What actually happens belongs somewhere in the middle.

entries.name: The Next Big Pivot: I Quit Following the Reclamation Campaign
entries: Even after Josric convinced me I could write my own adventures, part of my plan was still built around the idea that we would keep reclaiming sections of Bellwether. Different locations, different problems, increasingly powerful enemies. That was useful, but I was beginning to run into the same problem again: I was thinking about what the next chapter should be instead of what the people in Bellwether would actually do.

I wanted a bigger direction for the campaign. Not necessarily a bigger villain. I wanted the kind of change that would make everybody in the city have an opinion, even the people who would never pick up a sword.

Then I started thinking about Jarrock's future again. We already knew from Jill's story that Jarrock would eventually kill a King and Queen and take their child in. What was missing was the life Jarrock would have to live before that decision made any sense.

So I stopped thinking of the next adventure as another district to clear. I decided we were going to have a {@b Crown adventure}. Bellwether was going to go from a free city to a city ruled by a monarchy.

That was another actual pivot, not just a new subplot. {@i Ruins of Adventure} had already become a box of spare parts. Now the reclamation campaign itself was going to give way to something else. I would keep the places, people, maps and problems that still made sense, but I wasn't going to pretend we had to finish the old chapter order.
I did not decide what Jarrock would do about the Crown. I decided to give him a world where the question would eventually matter.

entries.name: The Most Ridiculous King and Queen I Could Take Seriously
entries: I also wanted the new royalty to be {@b comically evil}. Not secretly misunderstood. Not complicated villains who just needed somebody to explain their childhood trauma. I wanted the sort of King and Queen who could say something absolutely monstrous with complete confidence that they were being generous.

The trick is that nobody inside the world should be playing it as a joke. If an official announces that the citizens have been graciously relieved of their freedom and must now pay for the privilege, the official means it. The guards mean it. And the people who have to live under that decree can't just laugh it off.
That contrast is funny to me. A ridiculous premise taken seriously is a lot more interesting than everybody making jokes about how ridiculous it is.

The Crown also cannot explain everything wrong with Bellwether. People were cheating, stealing, protecting their families and abusing power before the royal banners showed up. Some people will do better under the Crown. Some will be crushed by it. Some will try to get on with their day.
There are still ordinary lives going on. I don't want Bellwether to stop being Bellwether just because the biggest people in it have changed.

entries.name: The Council Sold the City While You Were Doing Its Job
entries: Here is the part of the pivot I liked best: I didn't need to have an army march through the gates or make the King and Queen conquer the place.

The Council had already negotiated away Bellwether's independence. They had given you a legitimate job at Kellan's Well, and while you were out doing it, the city was being transferred to the Crown. The people running the city were allowed to make their own decisions while the party was elsewhere, and some of those decisions were awful.

I thought that was more interesting than telling the players they had somehow caused the takeover. You didn't cause it. You weren't even consulted. And once you got home, you would have to decide what to do about it.

Koven House would become the Crown's headquarters. The Council's old role as the organization handing out jobs was finished. Bishop Brann would remain in Bellwether. Brakkus would still have Ledger House. And the people who had spent the last few weeks rebuilding a free city would suddenly have to figure out who owned their work.

I also had an entirely different reason for wanting the change. Kaleb's death was still following Pepper around. The Council's punishment was one unpaid job, then four paid jobs. The new regime would complicate all that, and Kaleb's wife would become an indentured servant of the Crown. His adopted brother, Tulcornix Avemvir, could bring the party the news that she needed help.
That doesn't mean Pepper has to save her. It means the world did something with the consequences of Kaleb's death, and the next decision belongs to the players.

entries.name: Noren Told You Before Bellwether Could
entries: Before we sat down for Kellan's Well, I decided Noren was in charge of the Iron Covenant and was connected enough as a criminal to know what the Council had arranged. I meant to update the adventure notes but couldn't get the right file in front of me.
That turned out to matter. When Noren needed to save his own skin, he told the party the truth about the Crown. He was trying to make you question what you were doing and whom you were doing it for.

So the big reveal changed shape. Instead of learning for the first time when you walked through the city gates, you could come home knowing what a criminal had claimed and find out whether he was telling the truth.

I like that better than an NPC giving a speech about what has happened. Noren had his own reasons to talk. You had your own reasons to doubt him. Nobody needed to deliver an exposition dump because the next chapter was supposed to start.
More importantly, I didn't have to protect a scripted surprise by pretending Noren was too stupid or too poorly connected to know something he reasonably would have known.

entries.name: What Kellan's Well Actually Looked Like When You Played It
entries: The funny thing about Kellan's Well is that you guys solved some of the hardest problems without doing what I expected. You used {@spell Tasha's Hideous Laughter|XPHB} to stop the runner before the alarm went off. You used {@spell Fog Cloud|XPHB} in the Bow Gallery so the Rangers couldn't see you crossing the room.

Aaron read the surface thoughts of one of the Rangers. I got to have the Ranger say one thing, then tell Aaron what he was actually thinking. His words and his thoughts didn't match, and you learned something useful about where Noren was.

Then Arunem broke through the ceiling to get around Noren and his Veteran. That is not something I could have written as the one right way to get into that fight. It worked because he looked at the place as an actual place, not just squares on a map.

Pepper, meanwhile, had decided that if the Council wasn't paying her, she was going to find her own compensation. She searched enemy barrels, bodies and chests, and at one point she went for a chest instead of helping fight. Pepper is a cleric. That is what made the choice particularly funny.

And she was still angry with Jarrock for telling the Council about Kaleb. So she was refusing to heal him. Jarrock's response was basically, 'I was just keeping it real.' Both players were laughing. I couldn't have scripted their argument, and I wouldn't want to.

You also decided Jarrock was going to get drunk before work. Brakkus gave him a chance to change his mind, and you stayed with the decision. The disadvantages that came with it didn't make you stop playing Jarrock. They became part of playing him.
I have been saying I want the decisions to matter. That session gave me a whole lot of examples of what I mean.

entries.name: The Things You Are Learning Without Me Giving a Lesson
entries: Something else happened in those sessions that I didn't expect to enjoy as much as I do: I'm watching you work through consequences that are a lot closer to real life than hit points and treasure.

Jarrock told the truth about Pepper. I think there was a good reason to do it. That didn't mean Pepper had to be happy with him afterward. You got to see that you can do what you think is right and still have somebody be angry at you.

You also got to choose something fun for Jarrock and see that being drunk made doing his job harder. I didn't have to announce that drinking has consequences. Jarrock made the choice and had to deal with the result.

I'm not trying to turn our Sunday game into a lecture. I want you to have room to decide what Jarrock believes, make mistakes, defend your choices, and occasionally discover that the consequences aren't quite what you expected.
And I get to see that happen while we're all having fun. That's a pretty great thing to share with my son.

entries.name: Years of Fun Sundays
entries: After Kellan's Well, the players started talking about wanting to reach level 20. I pointed out that a campaign lasting that long could take years.
The response was, 'We'd have something fun to do on Sundays.'

I liked that more than somebody telling me I had built a good encounter. It meant you weren't just waiting to see how the next fight turned out. You could imagine us doing this together for a long time.

I'm still figuring out how to be a better DM. I want to build things that are ready to run, and I want enough freedom to change them when you guys do something I couldn't predict. Those goals aren't opposites. That's the job.
We may or may not ever reach level 20. I don't need that answer right now. The part I don't want to forget is that you guys thought years of Sundays sounded like a good idea.

entries.name: Why I Am Keeping These Notes
entries: This is the first full campaign I have ever run for you.
That matters to me.
I do not just want to keep a record of Session 1: this happened. Session 2: this happened. Session 3: this happened.
I want you to be able to see the campaign changing while we played it.
I want you to know that Osric existed before Milton.
I want you to know what the Silent Vault was supposed to be.
I want you to know that I went digging through old D&D adventures because I was trying to figure out the best way to build the kind of campaign I wanted.
I want you to know why Under Illefarn almost became the beginning.
Why the Slave Lords had ideas I liked but the wrong structure.
Why Bloodstone was too big too soon.
Why Princes of the Apocalypse almost worked but would have made the campaign about something I did not actually care about enough.
Why Ruins of Adventure finally gave me the structure I needed.
Why Brakkus is standing behind the bar at Ledger House instead of still being my character at Hall of Heroes.
Why Jarrock's future with Jill started changing the themes I wanted to explore.
Why Jarrock going down in one fight changed a rule we use at the table.
Why Pepper murdering one guy turned into something I may still be dealing with twenty sessions later.
Why Josric Pickle, who is not even in this campaign, changed how I thought about writing it.
Why I eventually stopped asking what the old adventure said should happen next.
Why Perrin became more complicated.
Why Tyren became a dragon.
Why I stopped treating reclamation as the whole campaign and turned it into a Crown adventure.
Why I wanted the King and Queen to be ridiculous while the people who lived under them took it seriously.
Why Noren warned you about the takeover before you even got back to the city.
Why I remember a fog cloud, a disabled runner, somebody breaking through the ceiling, and Pepper choosing a chest over a fight.
Why I was so happy to hear that years of playing D&D sounded like fun Sundays.
And why there are still going to be people in Bellwether doing completely ordinary things that have absolutely nothing to do with any of them.
Because that is the part I think will be easy to lose later.
When a campaign is finished, everything tends to look intentional.
It starts looking like the story was always headed exactly where it ended.
It was not.
This thing has already changed a ridiculous number of times.
It is going to change again.
Some of those changes will come from me.
Some will come from the other players.
Some will come from a die hitting the table.
And some will come from you deciding that Jarrock does something I never considered.
That is not you messing up my story.
{@b That is how we are making it.}

data.name: Appendix I: Current Canon and Session Record

entries.name: Authority and Use
entries: This appendix is the authoritative record of what has happened at the table through Kellan's Well, plus explicitly approved future premises. If an unplayed chapter contradicts a recorded fact here, this record wins. The older chapter may still be used for its map, encounter, location, or clue structure, but its obsolete political assumptions are not facts about the current world.

ESTABLISHED means played or explicitly decided. PREPARED means a future premise is approved but has not yet happened. PROVISIONAL means remaining design scaffolding, not fate. Do not present provisional material as something the characters have already caused or discovered.

{@b World independence.} People have jobs, families, feuds, ambitions and ordinary problems that continue whether the adventurers visit or not. Some events have no connection to Tyren, Perrin, the royal family, or the party. Do not make every clue secretly part of a single conspiracy.

{@b Player agency.} Move a clue when plausible, never move a consequence backward in time to force a conclusion. The party can outmaneuver opponents, abandon a location, negotiate, seek a different patron, or decide who deserves help.

entries.name: Established: Blackstone and the Council
entries: At Blackstone Temple, the party freed seven captives, confronted and killed Tal Rusk and remaining guards, recovered the reliquary, and returned it to Bishop Brann. The coded ledger, spyglass, and compass passed into Council custody. The party advanced to level 4 after Blackstone.

The Council confronted Pepper about Kaleb's death. The result was five compulsory missions: Kellan's Well unpaid, the remaining four paid; refusal carries the threat of jail. The rest of the party was not automatically sentenced.
The Council's independence transfer had already been arranged before the party departed for Kellan's Well; the party neither negotiated it nor caused it.

entries.name: Established: Kellan's Well, October 11
entries: The party approached the alarm runner as a tactical problem and used {@spell Tasha's Hideous Laughter|XPHB} to incapacitate the runner before it raised the alarm.
The party used {@spell Fog Cloud|XPHB} in the Bow Gallery to obstruct the Rangers' vision while crossing the defended room.

Aaron used surface-thought reading on a Ranger. The defender's spoken responses hid his purpose, while his thoughts revealed information about Noren's position and his determination to keep the party delayed. Distinguish spoken words and surface thoughts, not telepathic omniscience.
Arunem broke through the ceiling to outflank Noren and his Warrior Veteran instead of following the expected approach. Respect plausible use of the environment.

Noren was established as the connected criminal in charge of the Iron Covenant. To save himself, he told the party about the royal takeover. This was an intentional pre-session decision, not an accidental premature reveal; the next chapter confirms his warning.

Pepper, a cleric, searched enemy chests, barrels, and bodies for salvage because her Council mission was unpaid; at one point she chose a chest over helping in the fight. She loots enemies, not uninvolved civilians.

Jarrock chose to drink before work and continued after Brakkus gave him a chance to reconsider. He experienced the functional penalties of intoxication. Pepper refuses to heal Jarrock because he reported her involvement in Kaleb's death; Jarrock answers, 'I was just keeping it real.' The players have treated this conflict humorously; do not impose a mandatory reconciliation.

The party recovered the Decanter of Endless Water. Keep any unconfirmed claimed coin totals, expenditure, and consumable uses in player inventory rather than declaring that every listed treasure was collected.
The party's end-of-Well level is not recorded as increased beyond level 4. Do not automatically award level 5 by treating an unplayed older Koven House chapter as completed.

CORRECTED ACTUAL TABLE STATE: The party did not restore the main sluice, and the DM explicitly REMOVED sluice restoration from the campaign's pending objectives. The Well mission is complete for purposes of the Council contract, with Noren and one Veteran restrained during the short rest at the start of Session 4. Only three Bow Gallery Scouts were encountered; the alarm remained silent.

entries.name: Prepared: The Changed City
entries: Bellweather was a free city; the former Council sold its independence to a monarchy while the party was occupied. The royal rulers are comically evil in premise, but their subjects and officials treat the government as real and consequential.

Koven House is the Crown's local headquarters. Bishop Brann remains; Brakkus and Ledger House are independent. The former Council has left government in the city, so old chapters' references to the Council commissioning jobs after the takeover are no longer automatically true.

The return from Kellan's Well is a roleplay-led session without planned combat. Brakkus must sit the whole party down and ask about their backgrounds and goals; Jord and Bishop Brann participate as people with their own concerns; Tulcornix's arrival is a mandatory late-session beat. Fights only follow credible player choices and NPC responses.

Kaleb's wife has become an indentured servant of the Crown. His adopted brother Tulcornix Avemvir, an aarakocra, must personally arrive this session with the news that she needs rescuing. His arrival is guaranteed but Pepper's feelings and the party's decisions are not predetermined.

{@b Locked Pepper handling.} Pepper's four remaining paid service obligations imposed by the old Council are unresolved, NOT dismissed or automatically transferred into Crown missions. Brakkus stops supervising her former-Council house arrest and does not volunteer her case to the Crown; Jord can suggest staying under the radar. The Crown's administrative workload means nobody is currently prioritizing the case. No automatic arrest timer, offscreen warrant, forced service, or compulsory legal-hearing subplot. Future attention requires a credible in-world cause or player action.

Brakkus, Crown officers, merchants, tradespeople, former officials, and ordinary residents each pursue their own interests. The city reacts to the change but is not a single uniform opposition faction.
The players expressed interest in eventually playing to level 20, but no campaign extension, milestones, or finale level has been approved. The current 3–16 outline remains a planning framework only.

PREPARED START: open in Kellan's Well with Noren and his veteran captive, alive and tied. Killing Noren or turning him over to city guard removes him from the campaign permanently; releasing him sends him underground with the Iron Covenant network, potentially useful to resistance later. Then the party chooses its activities in Bellweather.

PREPARED FAMILY: Kaleb's widow Elowen is indentured in a Crown-administered textile annex at Cardon Weavehouse; Crown asserts 200 gp to discharge its manufactured bond (150 gp charge plus 50 gp fee). Her daughter stays safely with a trusted local neighbor. Tulcornix worked loading cargo near her and suffered a broken wing from a shifting loom beam. His arrival late this session is planned; healing his wing does not free Elowen. The deeper Weavehouse occupation and ownership from old Chapter 8 are still provisional.

SESSION 4 PREP (October 16, 2026): House Stucky = King Hendrix (competent, dangerous, stays in capital; no planned appearance), son Prince Reginald (Bellweather's ruler) and Reginald's wife Princess Narcissa (co-ruler). Former Council received money, land elsewhere and ducal titles. Royal transition became official while the party was in the Well for just a few hours, with advance preparation explaining the visible changes.

SESSION 4 PREP (October 16, 2026): Jord comes to Ledger House seeking lodging after royal guards commandeer his hotel. Bishop Brann seeks Brakkus and brings 300 gp owed by the Council for Kellan's Well: 100 gp each Jarrock, Aaron and Arunem, 0 gp Pepper. Distinct from the 300 gp Blackstone reliquary reward and from Well treasure. Brakkus's full history is already recorded.

SESSION 4 PREP (October 16, 2026): Tulcornix knows Pepper murdered Kaleb and deliberately seeks her. His direct line is 'You killed my brother, the stain of his blood will never leave your hands, save his wife and you might cleanse your soul.' Elowen's 150 gp retroactive municipal-services assessment and 50 gp discharge fee can be challenged, paid or subverted. Shops' differing reactions are in Appendix J.

LOCKED SESSION 4 ENDING (October 16, 2026): Tulcornix's arrival and direct accusation against Pepper are the LAST moments of Session 4. He reveals Elowen's plight at Cardon Weavehouse and the session ends immediately. The party's reaction, any detailed questioning, bond discussion or rescue is Session 5. The Cardon annex reference in Chapter 6 supports Session 5 or an unanticipated EARLIER discovery—not continued play after his arrival.

SESSION 4 OPENING CHECK: Brann's Council payment is owed for the completed Well mission without any sluice repair. The party starts during its short rest with the prisoners bound and no missing fourth Scout or mandatory maintenance action.

SESSION 4 PLAYTEST CONTINGENCY: Jord and Brann independently visit Ledger House, but may not be witnessed if the party never returns. In that case Brann keeps undelivered 100 gp shares; Jord still finds lodging. Do not force guest appearances into remote locations. Tulcornix seeks Pepper and ends the session when he finds her.

SESSION 4 PLAYTEST ADDENDUM: If the party attacks Koven House, use Chapter 6's finite defense (six Guards and one Veteran on station) and realistic alarm and travel. The resulting pursuit or custody is based on the NEW offense, not Pepper's unresolved Council contract. If the party's actions physically preclude Tulcornix reaching Pepper before the end of the evening, do not manufacture a prison visit simply to force the cliffhanger.

KOVEN ASSAULT PLAYTEST: Local garrison mapped to Koven House area 1, central room 6, side room 11, and west interior 20/24 (six Guards + one Veteran total). No upper-floor guard post. Local men rally behind doorways and may withdraw; the party could beat all defenders and obtain actual transfer records. Royals are not physically inside the first-day administrative building. New waves need real messengers, routes and time.

entries.name: Unresolved Future Design
entries: Chapters 7–17 retain usable locations, maps, opposition, rewards, and connective ideas from the earlier reclamation plan; their governing authority, automatic Council contracts, Perrin's eventual office, and exact level progression require revision for the royal regime and player choices.

Do not assume the Crown is already overthrown, that the Council returns, that Perrin becomes First Councilor, or that Jarrock is fated to kill any particular king or queen. Those are possible future developments, not settled facts.

Do not retcon the independent Tyren and Perrin threads into the royal takeover or force every unrelated danger to be Crown-directed. Future adaptations must preserve the world as bigger than the protagonists.

data.name: Appendix J: Bellwether Shops and Inventories
entries: DM inventory reference for Bellwether. These inventories begin after the party's Kellan's Well expedition and are independent of the PCs' level, needs, and available gold. Prices use the normal-price column of the D&D Shop Catalog V2.0.2 (Refresh) where applicable; invented curiosities have DM-set prices. GP = gold, SP = silver, CP = copper. Quantities are physical stock at this snapshot, not permanent supply guarantees.

Sale procedure: quote the displayed price, decrease stock on sale, keep sold items sold until a believable resupply occurs. Goods not listed here can be ordered or searched for in the city if appropriate; this inventory is the merchant's opening stock, not a prohibition on the existence of other merchandise in the world. 'One crate/box/set' means one indivisible lot unless the merchant agrees to split it.

Magic pricing reference from the catalog: Common 100 gp, Uncommon 400 gp, Rare 4,000 gp, Very Rare 40,000 gp, Legendary 200,000 gp. The catalog prices spell scrolls by level separately (cantrip 50 gp; level 1 100 gp; level 2 250 gp; level 3 500 gp; level 4 2,500 gp; level 5 5,000 gp). Individual consumables below use their listed prices. Rarity prices are campaign shop prices, not guarantees of availability.

Merchant independence: their merchandise need not reference the Crown, Perrin, Tyren, or the party's current goals. NPCs have commercial and personal lives. Do not turn every strange object into a clue.

entries.name: Selling Loot and Trading Equipment — Session 4
entries: {@b 2024 PHB equipment resale.} Usable ordinary equipment sells for HALF its listed purchase cost. Trade goods and valuables (such as gems and art objects) retain their face value. Apply only to items the party actually collected, kept and brings to a willing buyer; undiscovered gear cannot be sold.

{@b At the table.} Joren Viton of the Two Hammers is the natural buyer for serviceable arms and armor, with Maten inspecting condition when needed. Standard examples at their listed shop prices: a 50 gp greatsword sells for 25 gp, a 50 gp longbow sells for 25 gp, a 50 gp heavy crossbow sells for 25 gp, a 10 gp shortsword sells for 5 gp, and a 50 gp chain shirt sells for 25 gp. These are resale values, not extra encounter treasure. A merchant need not accept unsafe, counterfeit or unusable gear.

{@b Well ledger distinction.} The site contains 375 gp in fixed money/valuables, including 75 gp of salvage valuables. The valuables portion is already counted at its face value; DO NOT half it again or count it twice. The Well's confiscated weapons are separate physical gear that may have resale value if the party actually kept them. Don't automatically credit the party every weapon from every defeated defender.

{@b Magic and unusual property.} Magic item purchase costs follow the established campaign shop catalog. Do not infer a guaranteed half-price magic buyback from the ordinary-equipment rule; buyers can quote a price for a specific item. Keep each merchant's stock persistent, honor Jord's party discount when buying from him, and record actual completed sales.

entries.name: What Merchants Say About the Takeover — Session 4
entries: The adventurers spent only a few hours at Kellan's Well; merchants have just received public news of the transfer but may have seen preparations before. Shopping and asking questions are the SAME play activity, not separate scripted scenes. All can identify Reginald and Narcissa as the new royal governors, their father King Hendrix, Crown headquarters at Koven House and the departure of the Council. Only insiders have precise transfer terms. Their inventories, stock counts and existing personalities are unchanged.

TIERA DAME, THE TINY MAGE: Friendly, quick, observant, knows Pepper from Session 1. Saw work crews, flags and unfamiliar wagons even before the proclamation; she doesn't know the sealed negotiations. 'Prince Reginald and Princess Narcissa, they say. Funny thing, those fellows knew exactly where to hang the banners before anyone told us.' On closures: 'I'm open, aren't I?' Her other gossip need not connect to the Crown.

EDDA PELL, THE SPARE BUTTON: Dry, exact, practical. A clerk has started demanding shop licensing information, but she doesn't yet know whether the old license is void. 'A man wanted to see my trading license. I told him I've been here twenty-three years. Apparently that wasn't the question.' She sells the same buttons, magic items and scrolls, no invented magic ban.

JOREN VITON, THE TWO HAMMERS: Outgoing, sees royal guard purchasing as possible legitimate business. 'Soldiers break weapons. Someone has to repair them.' MATEN: Measured, uneasy about who will use his work. 'They've already got swords, Joren.' Joren: 'Swords break.' Neither knows the new army's confidential orders, and neither is automatically resistance.

JORD, JORD'S ODDS & ENDS: His hotel room has been commandeered to quarter the royal guard. 'Apparently a royal guard needs my room more than I do. Very apologetic, right up to telling me to move.' He plans to rent a room at Ledger House. If asked about Pepper's Council obligation, he recommends keeping under the Crown's administrative radar, not assuming legal forgiveness. His promised party discount is 20% off listed regular asking prices, recorded in Jord's inventory entry.

COMMON QUESTIONS: 'Who rules?' Reginald and his wife Narcissa govern for King Hendrix in the capital. 'Where are they?' Koven House is headquarters, not a guarantee of an immediate royal audience. 'What did the Council get?' Rumors of money, estates and new titles; insiders/records needed for confirmation. 'How did all this happen in a few hours?' Troops, supplies and paperwork were already in place. 'Do our old licenses, punishments or contracts still apply?' The Crown is sorting them through the Koven House registry, with no blanket cancellation. 'Are these the same guards?' Some former watchmen remain; royal soldiers are newly present. Public facts need no check.

One merchant can be pleased about a new customer, another annoyed about permits, another worried about safety. They have unrelated errands and personal lives; not every statement is a clue or a reliable fact. Don't invent a new mandatory tax decree beyond the prepared Royal Municipal Recovery Assessment.

entries.name: The Tiny Mage — Tiera Dame
entries: General store in the Slums. Despite its name, it sells everyday merchandise rather than magic. Tiera Dame is a 48-year-old halfling woman, small even by halfling standards, with curly auburn hair, dark-brown eyes, a green vest under her practical apron, and keys and small pouches at her belt. She is friendly, quick-speaking, observant, slightly gossipy, and suspicious of people who watch the shelves more than the price tags. She sorts stock while speaking. Her attention to local comings and goings makes her a useful neighbor, not a professional informant. Pepper met her during Session 1, when she warned about thieves in the Slums.
Portrayal cue: "Want fifty feet of rope? Had somebody buy three hundred feet last week. Never did find out why. Anyway, one gold."

entries.name: The Tiny Mage: Odd Warehouse Lot

entries.caption: The Tiny Mage: Odd Warehouse Lot
rows: Taxidermied goose in a removable judge's wig
Crate of 73 assorted LEFT boots, no right boots
Box of 400 one-inch carved wooden ducks
Brass ship's bell missing its clapper
Wedding cake topper depicting two ogres
Portrait of an unidentified man labeled 'Gerald'
Enormous brass key, unknown matching lock

entries: Odd-lot policy: Tiera bought a warehouse lot cheaply. She does not know why these objects were manufactured and has no special reason to think they are enchanted, cursed, prophetic, or related to the main plot. Most are mundane. If the players find clever practical uses for them, adjudicate normally. Some items can sell permanently out and be replaced later by wholly different junk.
If asked why she owns these: "Bought a warehouse lot. Got a good price."

entries.name: The Spare Button — Edda Pell
entries: Arcane merchant and genuine magic shop occupying a former sewing store. Edda Pell is a 54-year-old half-orc woman with short graying hair, round spectacles, rolled-up sleeves, and an apron with more pockets than should be necessary. She is practical, sharply observant, and dry-witted; sells remarkable enchantments as if they were household hardware. She did not replace the old sewing-shop sign because a new sign costs money. The wooden tray of ordinary buttons by the till remains for sale at 3 cp each.

Portrayal cue: "It flaps. Even indoors. Apparently somebody thought that was worth enchanting." (describing a Cloak of Billowing.) She bargains when given a sensible reason, describes what she knows accurately, and treats nobles and dockworkers alike.

entries.name: The Spare Button: Arcane Materials and Services

entries.caption: The Spare Button: Arcane Materials and Services

entries.name: The Spare Button: Spell Scrolls and Potions

entries.caption: The Spare Button: Spell Scrolls and Potions

entries: Buying magic is ordinary commerce here, not automatically a quest. The costly Ring of Spell Storing is a legitimate for-sale item even if the party cannot afford it. Magic stock is limited and replaced by real acquisitions, not convenience-driven refreshes.

entries.name: The Two Hammers — Joren Viton and Maten
entries: One shared weaponsmith/armorer business, not two separate shops. Joren Viton (human man, 43) is broad-shouldered with a neatly trimmed dark beard beginning to gray and tidy work clothes. Outgoing, commercial, honest, fast-moving, and enthusiastic about ready-stock equipment. He manages sales, prices, ordinary weapons/armor, and special orders. Maten (dwarf man, 112) is a muscular, gray-bearded master smith with thick eyebrows, scarred hands, and a permanently soot-stained apron. Quiet and exacting, he examines a weapon's balance and a client's grip before offering custom work. He is Bellwether's best armorer/weaponsmith. They respect one another: Joren keeps the operation profitable; Maten keeps its reputation.
Joren portrayal cue: "If you need it today, I have exactly what you need." Maten portrayal cue: "Want a sword made for you? Fine. Show me how you hold one."

entries.name: The Two Hammers: Ordinary Weapons and Ammunition

entries.caption: The Two Hammers: Ordinary Weapons and Ammunition

entries: Ordinary Scale Mail is always listed separately from the Mithral Scale Mail. The nonmagical suit provides AC 14 + DEX modifier (maximum +2) and imposes Stealth disadvantage under the game's standard armor rules. Mithral Scale Mail is magical, removes its normal Stealth disadvantage, and otherwise uses the armor's normal AC.

Commissions: custom or specially fitted ordinary gear is approximately +50% of the catalog's normal price and takes 1–3 weeks, according to complexity and workload; Maten can refit armor for different body plans. His superior workmanship does NOT automatically produce +1 attack, damage, or AC. Enchanted inventory above is acquired merchandise; neither smith must be an enchanter. Magical commissions are not automatically available.

entries.name: Jord's Odds & Ends — Jord
entries: Jord is an 86-year-old gnome traveling merchant with sandy, untidy hair, large expressive eyebrows, spectacles sliding down his nose, a patched good-quality coat with too many pockets, broad work-worn shoulders, and the dust of the road about him. Cheerful, quick-talking, resourceful, and a shrewd bargainer; he rummages while he speaks. His wagon carries practical goods, trade-ins, curiosities, and the occasional extraordinary acquisition. The party recovered his stolen strongbox and missing horse; he already rewarded them and promised a discount on future purchases.
Portrayal cue: "I had two, sold one outside the city, and the other might still be—ah! There it is!"

entries.name: Jord: Magic in the Wagon — Opening Snapshot

entries.caption: Jord: Magic in the Wagon — Opening Snapshot
Jord: Oddities and Trade-ins
rows: Barrel of sixty pounds of salt
Locked wooden box, contents unknown to Jord
Pair of boots with mismatched heel heights

entries: Discount continuity, now set for Session 4: after the party recovered his stolen strongbox and missing horse, Jord promised a party discount. The operating rate is 20% off his listed regular asking prices, including listed magic stock; calculate at checkout and decrease stock normally. The discount does not oblige him to buy back items at full retail, or magically replenish stock. If a specific price was already negotiated at the table, honor that prior transaction.

Random acquisition policy: Jord's magical stock is genuinely random and is NEVER capped by the party's current level or funds. He can carry rare, very rare, or legendary items. High-powered acquisitions are saleable at real prices, not automatically restricted to quests. Stock is persistent; items depart when sold, traded, lost, or legitimately moved on. He normally has 2–5 magical entries after a meaningful resupply; reroll only new acquisitions, never his entire existing inventory. The Rare Daern's Instant Fortress in this opening snapshot illustrates that rule.

On each NEW magical acquisition, roll d100 for rarity, then choose or randomly determine an existing magic item of that rarity whose provenance and physical size fit the transaction. Consumables can use their specific catalog prices instead. The table is a stock-generation aid, not permission to replace old stock at every party visit. A result being very rare or legendary does not make it a plot hook. Players may be unable to afford the item until much later.

entries.name: Party Gear Snapshot (Advisory, Not Stock-Tailoring Rules)
entries: Arunem: regular Scale Mail, greataxe, four handaxes, Potion of Healing, Oil of Slipperiness, scroll of Lesser Restoration. Pepper: Chain Shirt, shield, mace, two shortswords, Decanter of Endless Water, Potion of Climbing, and additional salvaged weapons, Holy Water and Kaleb's notebook. Jarrock: Studded Leather, two scimitars, dart, Poisoner's Kit, Thieves' Tools, potion of Healing, and ordinary adventuring supplies. Aaron's current equipment is unknown. These are references only; the shops do not stock to party demand.

Rules reminder: a Chain Shirt is AC 13 + DEX (max +2) without Stealth disadvantage, Scale Mail is AC 14 + DEX (max +2) with Stealth disadvantage, and Studded Leather is AC 12 + full DEX. An ordinary suit of Scale Mail does not upgrade Arunem, who already has one. Do not mistake magic armor's listed rarity price for a full set of custom work.
Revisiting inventory: after a party visit, edit individual quantities in this appendix or record sales in session notes. This is a reference snapshot, not a synchronized transaction system.

trait.name: Aura of Protection
entries: While Brakkus is conscious, he and friendly creatures within 10 feet of him gain a +4 bonus to saving throws.

trait.name: Aura of Courage
entries: While Brakkus is conscious, he and friendly creatures within 10 feet of him can't be {@condition frightened}.

trait.name: Aura of Devotion
entries: While Brakkus is conscious, he and friendly creatures within 10 feet of him can't be {@condition charmed}.

trait.name: Purity of Spirit
entries: Brakkus is continuously under the effects of {@spell Protection from Evil and Good|XPHB}.

trait.name: Relentless Endurance (1/Long Rest)
entries: When Brakkus is reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, he drops to 1 hit point instead.

trait.name: Lay on Hands (80 HP/Long Rest)
entries: Brakkus has a pool of 80 hit points of healing. As an action, he can touch a creature and restore any number of hit points remaining in the pool. He can instead spend 5 points to cure one disease or neutralize one poison affecting the target.

trait.name: Fire Walker
entries: Brakkus can stand on and move across molten rock as if it were solid ground.

trait.name: Paladin Spellcasting
entries: Brakkus's spellcasting ability is Charisma (spell save DC 17, +9 to hit with spell attacks).
At will: {@spell Sacred Flame|XPHB}, {@spell Word of Radiance|XPHB}
1/Long Rest: {@spell Shield|XPHB} (from Magic Initiate)

Prepared Paladin Spells (use spell slots): {@spell Lesser Restoration|XPHB}, {@spell Zone of Truth|XPHB}, {@spell Beacon of Hope|XPHB}, {@spell Dispel Magic|XPHB}, {@spell Freedom of Movement|XPHB}, {@spell Guardian of Faith|XPHB}
Spell Slots: 1st level (4), 2nd level (3), 3rd level (3), 4th level (2)

action.name: Multiattack
entries: Brakkus makes two attacks with {@item The Appendix|NCFA}.

action.name: The Appendix
entries: {@atk mw} {@hit 12} to hit, reach 5 ft., one target. {@h}11 ({@damage 1d8 + 7}) slashing damage plus 2 ({@damage 1d4}) radiant damage.

action.name: Divine Smite
entries: When Brakkus hits a creature with The Appendix, he can expend a spell slot to deal additional radiant damage: 2d8 with a 1st-level slot, 3d8 with a 2nd-level slot, 4d8 with a 3rd-level slot, or 5d8 with a 4th-level slot. The damage increases by 1d8 against a Fiend or Undead, subject to the normal Divine Smite maximum.

action.name: Sacred Flame
entries: One creature Brakkus can see within 60 feet must succeed on a DC 17 Dexterity saving throw or take 13 ({@damage 3d8}) radiant damage. The target gains no benefit from Half Cover or Three-Quarters Cover for this save.

action.name: Word of Radiance
entries: Each creature of Brakkus's choice within 5 feet of him must succeed on a DC 17 Constitution saving throw or take 10 ({@damage 3d6}) radiant damage.

action.name: Sacred Weapon (Channel Divinity; 1/Short or Long Rest)
entries: As an action, Brakkus imbues The Appendix with positive energy for 1 minute. He adds his Charisma modifier (+4) to attack rolls made with the weapon, raising its attack bonus to +16, and the weapon emits bright light in a 20-foot radius and dim light for another 20 feet.

action.name: Turn the Unholy (Channel Divinity; 1/Short or Long Rest)
entries: As an action, Brakkus presents his holy symbol. Each Fiend or Undead within 30 feet that can see or hear him must succeed on a DC 17 Wisdom saving throw or be Turned for 1 minute or until it takes damage.

reaction.name: Shield (1/Long Rest)
entries: When Brakkus is hit by an attack roll or targeted by {@spell Magic Missile|XPHB}, he casts {@spell Shield|XPHB}. Until the start of his next turn, his AC becomes 29, including against the triggering attack, and he takes no damage from Magic Missile.
Brakkus is a roughly forty-eight-year-old half-orc, retired adventurer and mercenary, and level 16 Oath of Devotion paladin of Torm. He owns Ledger House in Bellweather and maintains it as a refuge.
Brakkus is a home-base NPC, not a companion character. His default priorities are protect civilians, stabilize downed allies, contain the threat, then defeat the aggressor.
Challenge Rating. The listed CR is provided for encounter-building purposes; Brakkus is a 16th-level paladin.

Tal Rusk is a compact, scarred dwarf and the Iron Covenant commander still inside Blackstone Temple. He presents as practical and controlled rather than theatrical.

At the start of Blackstone Temple he has four Guards under his direct command. His immediate priority is recovering the coded Iron Covenant ledger Pepper holds; he is willing to trade a full withdrawal for it and does not need to destroy Bishop Brann’s sacred records or harm the rescued captives to achieve that goal.

Noren Vale is a mid-forties half-elf with a rangy build, short graying hair, one old facial scar, gloves, practical weapons, and a battered coat over piecemeal armor. He commands the Iron Covenant position at Kellan's Well.
Noren is not suicidal. He holds the Well while it remains defensible, tries to withdraw once the position is clearly lost, and surrenders if escape is impossible.

Current Kellan's Well roster: Noren Vale and exactly one Warrior Veteran, with no Toughs or extra reinforcements. In Session 4 both begin alive and restrained, and their disposition remains the party's decision.

A lean Harengon scout wearing a short Iron Covenant tabard and courier's leather satchel. Its orders are to reach the ground-level alarm pull at F14, not to kill the PCs.
The courier is harder to stop than a normal Scout (22 HP), adds +2 to initiative through Hare-Trigger, and can use Rabbit Hop twice. The alarm still costs one Action once reached.

item.name: The Appendix
entries: You gain a +3 bonus to attack and damage rolls made with this magic longsword.
On a hit, the weapon deals an extra {@damage 1d4} radiant damage.
The Appendix was given to Brakkus Ledgerhelm by High Justiciar Vance Halford and named in honor of Elena's love of books.
The item does not require attunement.
